sources.title: Farza on building HeyClicky: post-and-move-on content, daily writing, and surviving as a founder
sources.originalTitle: Farza on Building HeyClicky, AI Hype & the Future of Startups
sources.summary: Farza explains how he builds and markets with a tiny team: AI builds in unfamiliar stacks, 15 minutes of daily free writing, and short unedited videos posted without checking results. He also shares how a public shutdown taught him that staying alive and ignoring outside opinion matter more than being the best.

principles.text: Post the content and move on; don't watch the numbers. Early results can't be judged and praise distorts your beliefs.
principles.quote: We hit send or post and we we click X. We don't look at it. Don't care.

principles.text: Make many bad videos before good ones. Post a short unedited video daily for 30 days, then study what got views.
principles.quote: Pull out your phone right now, open Instagram reels, click record, tell the world what you're doing in 30 seconds unedited, and click post.

principles.text: Write freely every day for 15 minutes; hooks and stories surface from the habit.
principles.quote: write every single day for 15 minutes straight.

principles.text: Judge your work by what you deeply believe, not by what the world says about it.
principles.quote: just because the whole world says that we're innovating doesn't mean anything you know.

principles.text: Companies die when founders stop; the winner is whoever remains standing, so stay alive and keep building.
principles.quote: this is a game of who remains standing, not who was the best, who was the most innovative.

principles.text: Build the product people use and let the work speak; skip competitor talk and milestone noise.
principles.quote: I just believe that a great company is built by a great product and that's all we should care about.

sources.title: Farza on building Buildspace: culture over content, following what's sick, and raising $10M inbound
sources.originalTitle: Farza Majeed on Building the Hogwarts for Builders and Dreamers & Raising $10M
sources.summary: Farza explains how Buildspace pivoted from homeschool software to a free school for builders by following what excited him rather than a problem statement. He covers culture as the moat, hyper-specific audiences, being particular about every word, separating emotions from metrics, and raising money by letting investors come to you.

principles.text: Follow what you think is sick first; time-box it about six weeks, then see what problem it actually solves.
principles.quote: I just pursued what I thought was sick and um I just said Team just trust me I remember I told the teams trust me for two weeks and two weeks this will show results

principles.text: Culture is the real differentiator; the content is nearly interchangeable.
principles.quote: we have content it's good content it's nothing special to be honest with you yeah it's a little bit better than other content but it's like not I don't know it's what it's fine right what's special is like that with the culture it's a game changer

principles.text: Be hyper-specific about your audience from the start; with a tiny team, focus is everything.
principles.quote: always be hyper specific from the start um if if you can't tell me exactly who you're building like three three levels in like 18 to 22.

principles.text: Seed users by going where the ideal user hangs out: custom landing pages for 20 college CS clubs.
principles.quote: we infiltrated these clubs by making them these landing pages and they were like well let's build space and I was like like are you in build space they're backed by YC and a16z

principles.text: Be ultra particular about where and how your brand is talked about; speak to your audience directly and consistently.
principles.quote: I've always been Ultra particular about where build space is talked about and how so that's why I owe it when we started I did it a lot on live streams I would do it myself on Twitch in front of thousands every weekend

principles.text: Track the graph but don't tie your emotions to it; when it's down, change what you're doing, not how you feel about yourself.
principles.quote: if it's not going every week that doesn't mean you suck like it just means that what you're doing sucks so like change what you're doing

sources.title: Farza on taking software to market: find the one-liner first, charge day one, post consistently
sources.originalTitle: How to Actually Take Software to Market in 2026 with Farza Majeed
sources.summary: Farza (Buildspace, Hey Clicky) explains how he picks ideas by their one-line hook, thinks about the story while building, and gets first customers through real people before social media. He argues for charging from day one, judging inputs over outputs, and treating daily posting as a lottery ticket.

principles.text: Don't build until you have the one-liner you'd stop scrolling for; think about the story while building.
principles.quote: I never build anything unless I know how to talk about it first.

principles.text: Retention beats virality: look at how many viral downloads stick, then talk to those users.
principles.quote: Virality means nothing actually.

principles.text: Charge from day one; a clear yes or no from paying customers is higher signal than free usage.
principles.quote: The best way to get people to pay money for stuff is to charge money for stuff.

principles.text: Get your first 10 customers offline by talking to real people, before investing in social media.
principles.quote: Most ideas I think to get your first 10 customers, thousand customers, not a thousand, but like your first 10 or 100 customers, I don't think you have to talk online at all.

principles.text: Focus on inputs (posts made, features shipped), not outputs (views); review metrics analytically on a cadence, not emotionally.
principles.quote: have focus on your inputs, not your outputs.

principles.text: Treat daily short videos as a free lottery; expect traction around the 200th video, not the 10th.
principles.quote: it's probably going to be your 200th video in which something works.

sources.title: How Farza restarted after shutting down Buildspace: daily shots, collaborators, HeyClicky
sources.originalTitle: How to start over after shutting down a $100M Company | Farza Majeed, Founder of HeyClicky
sources.summary: Farza explains why he shut down Buildspace instead of selling it, the 6 months of doing nothing that followed, and how he rebuilt momentum by shipping something every week. Covers how he picks collaborators and hires, how HeyClicky grew out of a throwaway side project, and how he thinks about money and happiness.

principles.text: Give a nagging doubt 6 to 12 months before shutting a company down.
principles.quote: you can't just shut down four years of work in like a couple of days. Like it makes no sense. And so I was like, let me give this let me give this like at least a year, like 6 to 12 months

principles.text: A disengaged founder can't fake it; a good team sees through you immediately.
principles.quote: it's even harder to run to fake running a company. Like you can't just like pretend like you're in it cuz then the people around you if you hire a good team like they're going to see through you immediately.

principles.text: When winding down, put real effort into placing your team; this was his biggest regret.
principles.quote: put in a ton more effort to make sure everyone gets placed in the right place after versus like everyone just kind of like having to like fend for themselves in a way.

principles.text: Rebuild momentum by taking many cheap shots: ship something weekly and show at least one person.
principles.quote: My only goal every single week was basically I have to make something and I have to just at least show one person.

principles.text: Pick collaborators first for how much you enjoy talking to them, then for real skill.
principles.quote: I just enjoy having a conversation with them. ... That's like 95%. ... They actually have to be like really good at whatever they do.

principles.text: Trial candidates for up to three months before hiring to see how you collaborate.
principles.quote: I will then bring people out hopefully two to three months and work with months. ... Forget three months with everybody before hiring them because then you get a much better sense of then how you collaborate

sources.title: Farza on buildspace: commit to one thing, design the core loop, build distribution first
sources.originalTitle: Farza Majeed: Founder of Buildspace | BuilderTalks #11
sources.summary: Farza Majeed (buildspace) tells his path from selling blank DVDs and clothes online to self-driving research to buildspace. He argues for committing to one endeavor so learnings compound, designing a tight viral core loop before writing code, and building distribution through content. Tech is only a tool for solving a problem.

principles.text: Commit to one endeavor for years; sustained grinding on the same thing teaches more than hopping between projects.
principles.quote: nothing will teach you more than just like grinding on the same thing every day for like three years like nothing will teach you more than that right

principles.text: Pivoting is fine if it stays related, so your learnings compound instead of resetting.
principles.quote: commit to one thing and then be okay with pivoting is because it's like you want your learnings to compound over time right

principles.text: Define the core loop (sign up, complete, post, repeat) before writing code; a tight loop drove growth.
principles.quote: just draw that circle on a piece of paper before you write any code

principles.text: Build distribution first with content people want, such as educational projects that capture emails and an audience.
principles.quote: we wanted to first build distribution so we built these kind of like pieces of content right where you could come learn about blockchain

principles.text: Talk to your users and follow what they ask for, even if it means an early pivot.
principles.quote: we just talked to our users and our user said we want to learn web3 that's it

principles.text: Technology has no value on its own; the value is the problem you solve with it.
principles.quote: there's no value to machine learning and just on its own right the value to machine learning is like what is a problem i can solve the machine learning that's actually useful

sources.title: Farza on launch videos: ship mini demos daily, track downloads not views
sources.originalTitle: This Is How You Should Actually Make Launch Videos
sources.summary: Farza (Hey Clicky, Buildspace) explains why launching in 2026 means posting raw demos constantly on algorithmic platforms instead of one polished launch. He covers scripting hooks, tracking conversion per channel, targeting small niche audiences, and hiring a filmmaker early.

principles.text: Treat launches as constant mini demos, not one big event; ship them as often as possible.
principles.quote: I'd rather call these demos instead of launches and I just love shipping just demos constantly.

principles.text: Judge a video by downloads and retention, not views; real users are what justify building.
principles.quote: it's because 7,000 people downloaded it, and about 100 people of the 7,000 kept on using it every day for 5 days straight.

principles.text: Use a repeatable hook structure: who I am, what's going on, what I'm working on, then show it.
principles.quote: My formula is always the same. >> Yeah. >> This is who I am. This is what's going on. This is what I'm working on. Let me show you.

principles.text: Aim for targeted views from the right niche, not virality; small targeted videos can generate real leads.
principles.quote: So, the goal of my goal is never to go viral. It's just I want to talk about what I'm working on and I want to make sure it's listened to by an audience that would be interested

principles.text: Channels convert very differently, so track per-channel conversion (e.g. a dedicated link-in-bio) and double down on the best one.
principles.quote: This YouTube video has 20,000 views. But do you know what the conversion rate on this video is? It's like 20% to them actually downloading the app.

principles.text: Hire a filmmaker early; code is easy to clone but an audience and community are not.
principles.quote: what's really hard to clone is the audience and the community that I built around what I'm doing and the energy around it.

sources.title: Buildspace: how Farza grew a tutorial site into a story-driven school with 100K+ students
sources.originalTitle: Buildspace: The $100M Startup Building Hogwarts IRL | Farza Majeed | EP33
sources.summary: Farza explains how Buildspace evolved from web3 tutorials into Nights & Weekends and a physical school by following its most motivated users. He covers selling a story instead of a community, building for shy beginners, hiring by conversation, and running a team with trust and no task board.

principles.text: Build the next product from your most motivated users: ask what they want after they finish.
principles.quote: we found that a lot of them wanted to keep going after nights and weekends we had nothing to do for them but that was not only our most valuable audience that was our most motivated audience

principles.text: Sell a story people can step into, not a community or a course.
principles.quote: I don't think we have a community I just think we have a story that we've loudly talked about and tell other people about and let them be a part let them be a character in the in the story

principles.text: Build for the unconfident beginners the market ignores, and design it for yourself.
principles.quote: it's always making stuff for the people that are already confident that are already like the doers and my thing is like I want to make it for myself

principles.text: Regularly make the team justify every product, and kill it if nothing changes.
principles.quote: if nothing changes I'm killing it I'm gonna shoot nights and weekends so I've been with a team every season I'm like give me 10 reasons we don't kill nights and weekends

principles.text: Hire through real conversation, not skill-set pitches.
principles.quote: a lot of times I got an interview and they'll just be like trying to tell me about their skill set I was like dude chill out like we just met like I don't care about it

principles.text: Run the team on trust: people state what they are doing, with no task board or top-down list.
principles.quote: I never show up on a Monday and have a list for people we don't have like a task management board

sources.title: Farza on finding ideas: forge them, iterate weekly, and write a one-liner your mom gets
sources.originalTitle: lecture #1 -- ideas
sources.summary: Farza's buildspace lecture on locking down an idea in week one. He argues ideas are starting points rather than good or bad, tells his Minecraft-tutoring-to-buildspace story, and gives a practical routine: write a plain one-liner, then post it publicly for feedback.

principles.text: There are no good or bad ideas; an idea is just where you start, so start somewhere.
principles.quote: I think that ideas in reality are just places where you start you know um it's just where you start your journey

principles.text: Great ideas are made by repeatedly hammering on a starting point, not discovered in one go.
principles.quote: great ideas are forged they are not found you don't find a great idea you actually make it happen

principles.text: Change and improve the idea a little every week so it evolves instead of stalling.
principles.quote: your idea should actually change in small ways every week you know it doesn't have to be the same thing over and over and over and over and over again

principles.text: Follow what excites you, because boredom is the main reason people quit.
principles.quote: the number one reason you're going to give up is because you stop being excited about it

principles.text: Test clarity with the mom test: your one-liner should be instantly understood by a parent or friend.
principles.quote: if you tell your mom dad or your friend about your idea they should instantly say I get it like I understand what you're doing

principles.text: Get the idea out of your head and in front of real people early to get feedback.
principles.quote: I want you to get it out of your head and into the real world somewhere in the real world

sources.title: How Farza pitched AI companies and got a $50k/month yes for Make Something
sources.originalTitle: figuring out a business model and a customer saying yes to $50k/month
sources.summary: Farza reflects on a week where he proposed that AI companies pay for teaching people to build real things with their tools, and one agreed to $50k/month. He covers staying authentic when sponsored, thinking in steps rather than ceilings, productizing teaching into software, and using weekly deadlines.

principles.text: Sell AI companies the missing piece: getting people to actually build real things with their tools, not just sign up.
principles.quote: just cuz you have a better tool doesn't necessarily mean that everyone's going to use that tool to do great things.

principles.text: Don't fixate on an idea's ceiling; grow step by step and push past each ceiling when you reach it.
principles.quote: once you reach the ceiling there is always a way where you can break past that ceiling usually.

principles.text: Protect authenticity when sponsors pay you; only promote tools you genuinely use and like.
principles.quote: I don't want to put out XYZ tool just cuz they they paid me money. I want to talk about XYZ tool cuz they're actually really great.

principles.text: Pay your own happy users to talk about their experience instead of hiring random influencers.
principles.quote: I believe in that idea that you should empower people who enjoy your thing to go and talk about it

principles.text: A recurring public deadline like a weekly live stream forces you to ship and improve every cycle.
principles.quote: I work really well with deadlines. And it's nice to have a deadline every Sat cuz every Saturday you're going to have hundreds of people showing up and they're going to want to learn stuff.

principles.text: There are no shortcuts to a great idea; more cycles of doing the work makes you learn and move faster.
principles.quote: The more cycles you put in, the more you'll learn and the more you'll uh adapt and the faster you can move, you know?

sources.title: Farza: How to build and monetize a first AI-made app with coding agents
sources.originalTitle: I teach my friend how to make his first internet $ with AI.
sources.summary: Farza live-teaches a college student to build a personal site, a paid journaling web app with accounts and Stripe, and an iPhone app using Lovable, Replit and Claude Code. The takeaways: AI agents collapse build cost, ideas can be small and already exist, and a few paying users is a real win.

principles.text: You don't need a novel idea. Build something useful that you personally enjoy.
principles.quote: you don't need a crazy innovative idea, you just need an idea that you enjoy that's useful to you.

principles.text: Set a tiny revenue target. About 25 people paying $10 a month is enough to start.
principles.quote: you don't need to make a big idea, you just need to make an idea that can get 25 people to check it out.

principles.text: Don't skip an idea because the category is crowded. Make a version for yourself and your niche.
principles.quote: a lot of people say the app already exists. Who cares? Just make it.

principles.text: Software economics favor builders: pay to build once, then sell to many.
principles.quote: What's beautiful about software is you make it once and you can give it to everybody.

principles.text: The gap between people doing great things with AI and everyone else is knowledge, not talent.
principles.quote: it feels like the only thing that separates someone who's doing cool stuff with AI and someone who's not is just knowledge.

principles.text: Prompt agents like you'd brief a human engineer, then expect to iterate and test it yourself.
principles.quote: You should describe what you want kind of like you'd be asking a real human being.

sources.title: Solo founder lessons: shipping dead ideas, user calls, and loneliness
sources.originalTitle: being a solo founder is tough
sources.summary: Farza recounts a week where a shelved idea (Clicky) went viral while he felt lonely building solo. He explains why he ships stale ideas, values usage over views, calls top users to find direction, and assembles a small team rather than waiting for a co-founder.

principles.text: Don't let ideas rot on a shelf; ship them and see what happens.
principles.quote: I hate that feeling where it's like I feel like every idea should be just taken off the shelf and just thrown out into the world. And you just see what happens, you know?

principles.text: Usage matters, not virality or views.
principles.quote: views don't mean much to me. What mean What matters is like usage.

principles.text: When unsure, check top users in analytics and talk to them directly.
principles.quote: I looked at our top 25 users by usage um and I picked out 10 of them and I sent them all emails to my calendar and I said let's talk tomorrow.

principles.text: You can't predict who will use your product or why until it's out; let users reveal use cases.
principles.quote: As a founder, you have no freaking idea who's going to use your product and why they're going to use it until you put it out there.

principles.text: Treat user feedback as inspiration, not a spec to build one-to-one.
principles.quote: I just take feedback as inspiration. It's almost like I'm an LLM, and the users, when I talk to them, are prompting me.

principles.text: Drive forward yourself and let people join, rather than waiting for a co-founder.
principles.quote: I think that the best way to find people and to work with people is by just driving forward yourself. And as you drive forward, hopefully other people hop in your car as well

sources.title: Build education machines: AI + education should create human capital, not study tools
sources.originalTitle: Build education machines
sources.summary: Farza argues the biggest AI + education opportunity is end-to-end "machines" that take someone from a 2/10 to a 6/10 in their ability to pursue a goal, not tools that help students study. Pure learning is hard to monetize, while outcomes are what people pay for. AI could finally scale the accountability, structure and motivation that only high-touch human programs delivered.

principles.text: People learn in order to do something, so build for the outcome rather than the act of learning.
principles.quote: Very few people learn to just learn. They learn so they can _do_ something.

principles.text: Pure learning products cap out on monetization; people won't pay much or for long without a clear result in sight.
principles.quote: **And, you can only monetize straight up “learning” so much.**

principles.text: Reframe education companies as machines that build human capital, and judge them by how far they move a person on a 1-10 capability scale.
principles.quote: Machines where a person who is a 2/10 in their ability to impact the world + pursue their goals in some domain walks in, and can walk out at least a 6/10.

principles.text: Content doesn't transform people; the right mix of learning, accountability, structure and motivation does.
principles.quote: It’s offering the right balance of learning, accountability, and structure. All while properly maintaining your motivation.

principles.text: The best outcome machines are high-touch and human-led, so they don't scale. AI is the first chance to extend that access.
principles.quote: But for the first time ever, AI can change that.

principles.text: Build goal-specific end-to-end machines (YouTuber, author, coder, salesperson, filmmaker) instead of generic study tools.
principles.quote: It’s in building better end-to-end machines that output human capital.

sources.title: Money or dreams: why a short-term money printer and a generational vision must coexist
sources.originalTitle: money or dreams
sources.summary: Farza argues founders shouldn't choose between speed-running to $1M ARR on a thin AI wrapper and building a long-term dream; he wants both. Using his 2010 dropshipping days and the Nike story, he shows how a money-printing engine can fund a generational product, and urges founders to learn from winners instead of doubting themselves.

principles.text: Choose both: a money engine and a long-term vision. Don't shrink ambition just to hit a short-term revenue number.
principles.quote: I want to find the large opportunity and have the patience to build the dream, I don't want to lower my long term ambition just to hit a money number short-term.

principles.text: A great short-term money printer can become a generational product if paired with vision, so having the engine beats not having one.
principles.quote: I think a great short-term money printer has a high chance of turning into a generational product with the right vision. I'd rather have an engine, than not.

principles.text: Wrapper-style businesses die when arbitrage margins vanish; survivors build their own product, formula or secret sauce.
principles.quote: since nearly no one was focused on building a true product that'd become core to people's lives, most dropshipping businesses died except those that put effort into their own formula, product, secret sauce, etc.

principles.text: Anyone can copy the niche-wrap-distribute playbook; the winners are the obsessed ones with relentless execution and love for the game.
principles.quote: Anyone can wrap a model, just like anyone could dropship. But hitting $100K a month on anything is difficult as fuck -- it takes relentless execution and genuine love for the game.

principles.text: Nike began as a dropshipping wrapper for Onitsuka Tigers, funded growth, then moved to making its own product. Start with what works, then evolve.
principles.quote: Nike spent its first 10 years being a wrapper around Onitsuka Tigers from Japan just dropshipping their shoes. But, Phil Knight kept growing the biz, made a money printer, kept growing the vision.

principles.text: Don't let ego block tactics that work; when you see someone winning, ask what you can learn instead of what you're doing wrong.
principles.quote: When you open the internet and see someone winning online, instead of feeling like "Damn what am I doing wrong" think "What can I learn from this person and their work".

sources.title: Farza on why you don't need a vision to start a company, and how to earn one
sources.originalTitle: visions
sources.summary: Farza, founder of buildspace, explains why he stopped faking a grand "vision" in 2019 and admitted he didn't know where he was going. Honesty attracted teammates and investors who trusted a track record of doing what he said. A long-term vision is a skill built from years of immersion in one craft, not a flash of genius.

principles.text: You don't need a vision to start a company; admit what you don't know and invite people to figure it out together.
principles.quote: You don't need a vision to start a company.

principles.text: Honesty about not having a vision filters for the right people: those comfortable navigating the unknown.
principles.quote: I ended up attracting very different types of people... People that were down to navigate the unknown with me.

principles.text: Build trust through results, not persuasion: say you'll do something, do it, and report back whether you won or lost.
principles.quote: I had a long history of consistently saying I would do something, then doing it, and then updating people on results (whether I failed or succeeded).

principles.text: Long-term vision is a skill earned by repeated shipping in one craft, not something you can force.
principles.quote: You improve your ability to have a clearer view of the long-term by deeply immersing yourself in your craft. You can’t force a vision.

principles.text: Each cycle of making teaches you what to do next, so your vision for year 5 sharpens from years 1 to 4, and your ability to execute grows with it.
principles.quote: By Year 3, you’ve learned a lot from Year 1 + 2 and have a better “vision” for your Year 3.

principles.text: Don't pretend to be someone else; fix your flaws but stay yourself.
principles.quote: Focus on improving yourself and solving your flaws, but, never pretend to be someone.

sources.title: How Farza got a16z to invest $2M as a solo founder with no pitch
sources.originalTitle: How a16z ended up investing in us
sources.summary: Farza explains how a16z invested $2M in ZipHomeschool without a formal pitch or competitive process. He built in public, ran weekly progress calls with the investors, pivoted to a viral product, and let momentum do the selling. a16z later doubled down on buildspace.

principles.text: Build something cool and talk about it online; investors and helpers come to you.
principles.quote: My philosophy was if I built something really cool and talked about it online -- people would reach out + just invest in me.

principles.text: Be radically honest with investors, even admitting you're a noob. It doesn't kill interest.
principles.quote: when a16z asked me how much I was raising, I literally said that I was a noob.

principles.text: Skip the competitive fundraising game; weekly update calls let investors watch your progress build conviction.
principles.quote: I was told by many to not do this. To instead run a "competitive" process but I just felt that was dumb game.

principles.text: Weekly progress calls give investors more data on you while you keep building; the downside is you end up profitable.
principles.quote: it was perfect for me -- I could just keep building and if my co blew up up either: a) they'd probably invest: b) i just end up profitable lol.

principles.text: Don't use finding investors as an excuse for lack of progress. Put out great work to a growing audience over a long horizon.
principles.quote: In reality, you simply need to put out really good work to an audience that grows over a long horizon.

principles.text: Be willing to pivot hard; the pivot to live teacher streaming went viral and closed the round.
principles.quote: I pivot from legal software to building Twitch for teachers where teachers streamed classes live to thousands of kids.

sources.title: The founder spiral: why founders' mental downward spirals kill startups, and how Farza catches his early
sources.originalTitle: the founder spiral
sources.summary: Farza adds a third reason companies die beyond failing to raise or co-founder conflict: the founder slides into a negative mental spiral and can't solve daily problems. He explains how exhaustion compounds into irritability and self-blame, and shares his personal system for catching a spiral within 7-14 days and resetting.

principles.text: A third reason startups die: the founder spirals mentally, can't catch themselves, and eventually quits.
principles.quote: The founder simply ends up in a downward spiral, and can’t catch themselves.

principles.text: Poor sleep, food and movement leave you too tired to solve new problems, which feeds the spiral.
principles.quote: You don’t have the patience or mental strength to solve these new problems.

principles.text: Watch for early signals (quick annoyance at others, low energy), journal daily, and check in with yourself.
principles.quote: I also journal every day, and I even ask myself “am I spiraling?” a couple times a month just to check in.

principles.text: When you spiral: stop everything, admit it's okay, go home, and spend a day on energizing activities.
principles.quote: Admit to myself that I’ve lost to my emotions and am spiraling — and that’s okay.

principles.text: Catch spirals early; the longer you wait, the harder it is to climb out. Then return to eat, sleep, exercise.
principles.quote: The longer it takes me to recognize the spiral, the worse it gets, and the harder it is for me to muster the energy to get out of it.

principles.text: Founders are highly susceptible, so build an internal system that protects you from your emotions.
principles.quote: you need to build that internal system that protects you.

sources.title: Farza's dream team: a 3-month, time-boxed small team to find the next company
sources.originalTitle: dream team
sources.summary: Farza recruits four people (software, film, design, content) for a 3-month paid sprint in SF with no fixed idea. He lays out how he approaches the earliest, unknown stage of a company: a tiny team, daily shipping, ruthless ideas, and a hard deadline.

principles.text: At the earliest stage, don't pretend to have a grand vision; throw things out and see what resonates.
principles.quote: i am at that early unknown stage no one really talks about — where you are just throwing stuff out and seeing what resonates.

principles.text: Big companies start with a small group of like-minded people tinkering daily.
principles.quote: i believe in the power of a small group of like-minded people essentially tinkering daily. to me, this is where every big vision or big company starts.

principles.text: Run the early stage as a daily loop of inspiration, making, and sharing.
principles.quote: every day is about getting inspired, making something, sharing it, and trying to find something completely new together.

principles.text: Time-box the experiment: if nothing works by the deadline, disband the team.
principles.quote: and if in 3-mo we got nothing — then the team will self-destruct.

principles.text: Optimize for learning speed and shipping volume, not for looking cool.
principles.quote: the goal will be to learn fast.

principles.text: Staff a small team with complementary builder, design, film and virality skills.
principles.quote: i believe this group can build nearly anything, and take over the world together.

sources.title: How Farza and Julian got 35 people to their first $ in 3 days with live sessions and an AI chatbot
sources.originalTitle: Helping 35 people make their first $ in 3 days
sources.summary: Farza and Julian sold a simple 3-day live Zoom program (idea, small version, first dollar) via one LinkedIn post, making $1,400 in hours. The AI chatbot was hidden inside the program and used to surface mental blockers. The core lesson: people are held back by psychology, not knowledge, and the AI piece works best when packaged around a goal and done live with others.

principles.text: Most people aren't blocked by money, knowledge or motivation; they're blocked by their own psychology and limiting beliefs.
principles.quote: The main barrier people have is they don’t understand their own psychology. They have hundreds of mental blockers on why they “can’t” do something or aren’t “ready” to do something

principles.text: Only build and sell things you would personally use or convert on.
principles.quote: And I strictly believe to only put stuff that I myself would convert on or use.

principles.text: Package the product around an outcome people already want, not the technology. Don't sell the AI; sell the result.
principles.quote: No one wakes up and _wants_ to use AI for mental breakthroughs. So, why sell it when people don’t even know they want it? I rather package it differently.

principles.text: Validate by selling first: one LinkedIn post and a simple, easy-to-understand offer produced $1,400 within hours, before the product existed.
principles.quote: Instead, we sold a simple 3-day program.

principles.text: With bots, conversation quality is the product, so prime users on how to talk to it and make the AI use a shared, live experience.
principles.quote: With bots, the quality of the conversation _is_ the product. So anything that can make that feel better will make everything feel better.

principles.text: Give people a concrete goal and they'll work through whatever blocks them; live formats plus product are underexplored.
principles.quote: No one signs up for “builder therapy.” But tell them the goal is their first dollar in 3 days and they’ll work through whatever’s in the way.

sources.title: Farza on rejoining Y Combinator at 30: building again with hard-won experience
sources.originalTitle: I decided to join Y Combinator, again
sources.summary: A personal essay where Farza explains why he is joining YC a second time at 30 without a fixed idea. He contrasts the naivety of founding at 23 with the clarity of 30, and why he chooses to build over taking a safer job or VC path. Mindset-focused, with little tactical growth content.

principles.text: You will never feel fully ready to start a company, so go for it anyway.
principles.quote: I feel like I'll never be “ready” so just gotta go for it. Yolo baby.

principles.text: Pair beginner's naivety with the hard-won experience of having built before.
principles.quote: Still, I feel like I have the naivety of a 19 year-old, but, with the mental of a guy who’s been through a lot and learned a lot.

principles.text: You don't need a specific idea to start; act on the pull to explore your ideas to avoid regret.
principles.quote: it’s more a feeling of “I should explore my ideas...I would regret it if I didn’t”.

principles.text: Choose the riskier path of building when your vision keeps nagging you, even if safer jobs are on offer.
principles.quote: every time I think about getting a job (of which I’ve been offered many great ones) that voice in my head comes back and says to give my visions a shot.

principles.text: Timing matters: major technology shifts are the best moment to work on your ideas.
principles.quote: There’s never been a better time to work on the ideas in my head.

principles.text: Spend time building rather than documenting; keep updates lightweight.
principles.quote: I’m not going to spend a lot of time documenting. Will mostly be focused on building.

sources.title: Tidbit: how Farza and Sharif pivoted back to consumer instead of chasing B2B
sources.originalTitle: Tidbit has 7 more days left to live
sources.summary: Farza explains why he and his cofounder nearly pivoted Tidbit, then refocused on single-player consumer after realizing B2B wasn't energizing them. He covers time-boxed bets, rapid weekly rebuilds, TikTok content conversion numbers, and third-party validation of a cofounder pairing.

principles.text: Don't chase a big market you don't care about; you'll lose motivation and quit before it matters.
principles.quote: what’s the point of working on a $100M opportunity if I’m not motivated about the opportunity itself? I probably won’t even make it far + give up.

principles.text: Build products you use daily; losing that is a warning sign you've drifted from your core vision.
principles.quote: We looked up and realized we were no longer building a product that we were using daily.

principles.text: A good idea should survive a pivot discussion, and surviving it strengthens your confidence.
principles.quote: I think an idea should be able to survive a pivot discussion. If it does, can make your confidence in the idea stronger.

principles.text: Early in a company, the work should give you energy; don't tolerate depleting work this early.
principles.quote: when it’s this early in the product/company — I should be getting energy from it.

principles.text: Use real usage analytics to see who your actual power users are, even if they differ from your paying customers.
principles.quote: the users who were really using Tidbit like crazy were just normal people using it’s long-context feature for everything from #copywriting to #therapy to #tiktok-scripts.

principles.text: Prefer big weekly swings that test new hypotheses over small incremental changes on a flawed one.
principles.quote: We rather the app looking massively different each week and we test new hypotheses vs make a bunch of small incremental changes over a longer period on a flawed hypothesis.

sources.title: How Tidbit pivoted its messaging, used daily A+ goals, and built AI agents on webhooks
sources.originalTitle: Tidbit has 3-weeks left to live
sources.summary: Farza's weekly update on Tidbit, a multiplayer AI chat product. He covers setting one daily A+ goal for the team, pivoting positioning from "replace Slack" to "work better with AI" without changing the product, shipping webhooks and MCPs, and switching short-form video from Reels to TikTok to land B2B customers.

principles.text: Set one daily A+ goal so every day is a clear win or loss, never a confusing middle.
principles.quote: I really hate going home and not knowing if I won or lost. I want to know. If I won great I’ll come back and play even harder tomorrow.

principles.text: A hard deadline with the right goal gets product shipped fast.
principles.quote: It’s kinda beautiful how an intense deadline with the right goal can feel so good.

principles.text: Early on, fix messaging before product: choose the emotion users enter the tool with.
principles.quote: Early days, I think it’s about nailing messaging. And product doesn’t need to change much. Sometimes, it’s up just setting up messaging properly so the emotion people enter the tool with is a hyper-specific one.

principles.text: Pick messaging by combining what excites you as a user with what excites your audience.
principles.quote: I think its just up to us to see 1) whats the most exciting angle for us 2) what are the angles people most excited about. And properly combining both.

principles.text: Simple tweets about a feeling people already have beat product-pitch asks.
principles.quote: No one gives a shit about Tidbit. But, everyone knows how they feel when they think of Slack.

principles.text: Automate the manual founder work you already do, and make the agent visible to the whole team.
principles.quote: I was already doing all this manually. Every time a new user came in, I’d Google them to see if I wanted to learn more. Now I can just have a Claude agent do it.

sources.title: Why Farza ran a live stream instead of a launch: narrative-first marketing for Tidbit
sources.originalTitle: Why a live stream instead of a launch
sources.summary: Farza explains why he and Sharif used a live stream with a hard deadline to get Tidbit's first customers. He sets a small goal (10 paying teams), picks the narrative first, builds a simple landing page around it, and values the right audience over big view counts. The stream got 14 customers from about 14,000 views.

principles.text: Use a deadline you can't move as a forcing function; it extracts clarity and shipping fast.
principles.quote: We both really like deadlines where you can't push them and have to deliver else we'd end up embarrassing ourselves. Forcing functions are good.

principles.text: Set a tiny, concrete goal for a launch event: a number of paying customers plus a good demo.
principles.quote: Find 10 legit teams down to pay us $99 a month + do a good demo. That's it.

principles.text: Decide the narrative first. Find the story already in front of you and put it in words; never invent it.
principles.quote: The narrative is always the first thing I'll decide on. If the narrative isn't clear and the story isn't compelling, the audience will get confused, the story will get muddled, and people will lose interest.

principles.text: Choose narratives that are easy to latch onto and easy for people to retell to friends.
principles.quote: I like narrative's that are easy to latch on to and easy to talk about/tell your friends about.

principles.text: Prefer a small, engaged audience over viral reach. Views that don't convert mean nothing.
principles.quote: I rather find 10 people that genuinely give a fuck, really believe in the core idea + are ready to iterate with me, versus chasing 1,000 likes on a tweet or 1M on a video.

principles.text: Write landing-page copy you would convert on yourself; if you wouldn't pay, no one else will.
principles.quote: Most importantly, it felt like a landing page I'd convert on for $99 a month. If I wouldn't convert on it no one else would.

sources.title: How Farza and Sharif jumpstarted Tidbit in 14 days in Japan
sources.originalTitle: Jumpstarting Tidbit in 14 days in Japan
sources.summary: Farza recounts finding a co-founder in Sharif after five years solo, then flying to Tokyo with no idea to build. Daily prototypes, one-liner tweets, demo-driven development and rapid user calls turned into a product with paying customers and 1000+ DMs in two weeks.

principles.text: Try stuff to find stuff: build aggressively with no fixed plan and let experiments reveal the product.
principles.quote: Both me and Sharif have the same philosophies when it comes to building stuff — you gotta try stuff to find stuff.

principles.text: Test product vision by writing one-liners and launch tweets; if you both find it exciting, you're aligned.
principles.quote: if we could describe the idea in one line or make it sound exciting in a tweet — then we’d be on the same page.

principles.text: Run a tight daily loop: plan in a 30-60 minute morning check-in, ship by evening, and surface co-founder friction immediately.
principles.quote: Every morning around 9AM we’d spend 30-60 minutes to figure out what we wanted to do by 9PM.

principles.text: Make the goal a product you love using yourself, and optimize for learnings rather than vanity metrics.
principles.quote: We were optimizing for learnings. Not a user number, or a graph, or a money number.

principles.text: Ship demos daily and shamelessly, without polish; demos force clarity and attract the first real signal.
principles.quote: We also agree to start posting daily demos immediately. We were gonna be shameless. Didn’t care about polish.

principles.text: Talk to users to learn why they're excited; unexpected use cases from them shape the product for you.
principles.quote: My main goal of the convos was to get a clearer and clearer idea of why people were excited about it.

sources.title: How Farza starts from zero: 21 days of shipping daily and showing one person
sources.originalTitle: Starting from zero: 21 days in
sources.summary: Farza shares what he learned in his first 21 days starting over: no rules except show up daily and make something to show one person. Small, fun, unplanned projects (a text editor, a YouTube video, a voice agent) outperformed expectations, and showing work early fuels better ideas.

principles.text: Keep only two non-negotiable rules: show up every day, and make something and show at least one person.
principles.quote: But I am insanely, stupidly disciplined about two things: - Show up everyday. - Make something, show one person.

principles.text: Ship the small, niche, embarrassing thing anyway; expectations of near zero leave room for big upside.
principles.quote: Still was embarrassed at how simple, small, and niche it was. But, just decided I don’t give a fuck what people say let’s ship it.

principles.text: Make things because they seem fun and because you like the people involved, not for a master plan.
principles.quote: _I just did it because it seemed fun._ And 95% because I like working with Josh.

principles.text: Show rough demos to people immediately; their reactions trigger the next idea and reveal what's interesting.
principles.quote: When I show someone something, and they start telling me their thoughts, and then that triggers a new idea in my head, and all of a sudden it’s that feeling I know super well — like you’re on to something.

principles.text: Put your users in a single group chat; watching how they talk about the product generates ideas.
principles.quote: adding your users to a single GC is always a good idea. I always learn so much from just seeing how ppl talk about the product.

principles.text: Build with other people in small ways, even for 30 minutes, to gain energy and improve ideas.
principles.quote: I should build with other people even if it’s only like for 30m and even if I have barely any idea what I’m building.

sources.title: Why builders should tell their story weekly: how a newsletter led to a $25K first check
sources.originalTitle: A short post about investors
sources.summary: Farza explains why chasing investors early is a focus sinkhole, but ignoring capital entirely is also a mistake. His answer is to consistently "tell the world" over 12-24 months, especially via a weekly progress newsletter that builds trust with a small audience who may later fund you.

principles.text: Chasing investors early is usually a focus sinkhole, but fully ignoring money is also a mistake; set yourself up to get lucky.
principles.quote: I also don't think fully ignoring the money world is good either, you wanna set yourself up to get lucky + potentially pursue investors.

principles.text: Builders who raise money tend to be good at telling the world consistently over a 12-24 month horizon.
principles.quote: Those I see from buildspace that end up raising money magically, scoring a $25K grant, getting a small angel check, whatever often are just really good at "telling the world" consistently over a long horizon (ex. 12-24 months).

principles.text: Build trust with an audience over a long time rather than chasing one-off virality, which is hard to control and fades fast.
principles.quote: You wanna build trust with an audience over a long time.

principles.text: A weekly progress newsletter is the most underrated way to tell your story.
principles.quote: The most underrated way to "tell the world" your story is simply by writing a newsletter each week with your progress.

principles.text: Farza's own newsletter, written weekly for ~3 years to just 125 subscribers, produced the $25K that started his company.
principles.quote: I ended up building an audience of people that deeply understood me + my journey -- and when one day I needed $25,000 to start this company, I ended up getting it from one person on that newsletter.

principles.text: Prefer durable formats (newsletter, blog, monthly vlog) over ephemeral tweets so people can see your long-term history.
principles.quote: Something like a newsletter, blog, etc helps people see your long-term history + lets you communicate more thoroughly.

sources.title: Six months away after buildspace: recovering the spark after a company ends
sources.originalTitle: Six months away after buildspace
sources.summary: Farza writes a personal update after six months of travel following the end of buildspace. It contains no growth, marketing or pricing tactics, only a reflection on burnout, feeling like a flop, and rediscovering the joy of making things. Low durable business insight beyond a mindset lesson.

principles.text: Leaving a failed or ended company behind doesn't erase your problems; the sadness and self-doubt travel with you, and time does the healing.
principles.quote: you don't just get on a plane and have your problems disappear (would be nice)

principles.text: Founders are their own harshest critics, even when the outside world says you did well.
principles.quote: it was a good run. you gave it your best" but of course, you are always your worst critic.

principles.text: Burnout can make you fear you've permanently lost your love of building, but that spark can return.
principles.quote: i think what freaked me most was the thought that i’d never feel that love building stuff ever again.

principles.text: Recovery comes from stepping away and letting time pass, then re-entering by hacking on small ideas daily and rediscovering the joy of making things.
principles.quote: i think time just did what time does.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains how he builds and markets with a tiny team: AI builds in unfamiliar stacks, 15 minutes of daily free writing, and short unedited videos posted without checking results. He also shares how a public shutdown taught him that staying alive and ignoring outside opinion matter more than being the best.

chunks.heading: Early life: eBay, a $100K/year business at 15, and why he never got a job
chunks.text:
- Farza was born in Pakistan in 1995 and raised in Florida. His dad started as a New York taxi driver, then a Miami pizza maker, then a car salesman at Nissan from 1999 until he resigned in 2026.
- At 13, Farza got a job offer spinning a sign outside a gym ($12/hour). His dad refused: "You're smarter than that. You're more creative than that. You're not allowed to get a job."
- He noticed his family donating clothes once a year, asked to sell a $40 Calvin Klein shirt on eBay, and started a six-year online business selling blank media, clothes and other goods.
- The business existed to fund a YouTube channel: "I wanted a job so I can make cooler videos." Money went back into cameras, props and costumes, sometimes thousands of dollars a day.
- By 15 he was making about $100,000 a year, more than his teachers. That broke the "go to college to get a job that pays six figures" logic and showed him "you can live life however you want to live life and make your value however you want to make your value."
- His dad quizzed him at dinner every night ("How much did you sell this week? Why did it go down?"), which Farza describes as daily training, not pressure. Family rules were only three: no drugs or alcohol, no girls, straight A's.

chunks.heading: How he got into Y Combinator
chunks.text:
- In 2016-2017 he trained AI models for video games. One, which analyzed League of Legends gameplay, went viral, and "basically every technology company" (Google and most SF startups) tried to hire him.
- His plan was to graduate, then move to SF or New York to start his next company.
- A founder named Ivan, whose company was associated with Y Combinator (which Farza had never heard of), invited him to SF. He flew out within weeks, at age 22.
- At 24 he got into YC with Zip Homeschool, an online learning platform for homeschooled kids. It later pivoted into Buildspace.

chunks.heading: Lessons from Buildspace shutting down
chunks.text:
- Buildspace's shutdown was public and, he says, "fully me": he couldn't take it anymore and broke down "as if you're a fighter."
- He was obsessed with what people said about Buildspace; one bad comment would stay in his head. He was also constantly asked about competitors and the next milestone.
- He now refuses those questions: "A great company is built by a great product and that's all we should care about. Someone should grow the product and someone should build the product."
- His key realization: "Companies only close for one reason because the founder didn't want to do it anymore." You could have kept working at Starbucks and spent an hour a week on it.
- His resulting rule: only stop if you give up, and arrange life around not giving up. The game is "who remains standing, not who was the best."
- He says that had he kept Buildspace alive, "it'd be doing so much better just cuz I stayed alive," because work compounds when you keep building on it.
- Practical mindset: after 16 weeks of no growth you can be upset or just ask "what are we doing next?" He compares it to staying calm rather than losing sleep.

chunks.heading: Building HeyClicky: demo, team, and tools
chunks.text:
- Clicky began as a solo demo that went viral. He then asked friends and colleagues to fly to San Francisco and turn it into a company in six weeks.
- The OG team came from Poland, India and Peru. Jose, from Peru, built an open source fork of Clicky that had about 12 views on Twitter. Farza was impressed, FaceTimed him while Jose sat in his car in Texas, and asked if he'd fly to SF the next day. Jose said yes.
- He built the team because "if I worked on stuff alone... I wouldn't have the same energy."
- He built Clicky because "nothing else existed for me": "everyone's circle jerking themselves about AI and then I didn't find a single product I enjoyed using."
- Tech approach: he doesn't know Swift, so the product is generated code plus all-day prompting (the landing page was handmade). He uses whichever model is best at the moment (Claude now; GPT-6 or Grok's coding tool when they're better).
- Favorite product-ideation flow: take something he loves from the product, put it in Claude Code or another strong model, and ask it to brainstorm why he likes it and how to build a fresh version of it into Clicky.
- Internal tool "Black Hole": all company data (meeting transcripts, messages, everything) is dumped in and organized by an agent like a Wikipedia (successor to his earlier Farzipedia). The team asks it things like "five really cool hooks for videos based on what users are actually telling us."
- Product goal: "make the simple things magical for you."

chunks.heading: Making content: write first, post, then move on
chunks.text:
- Posting policy for himself and the company: hit post on X, don't look at the results, and immediately ask about the next video. Results take 24-48 hours, so checking is useless. If everyone loves it, "who cares? They were meant to love it if we thought it was cool."
- Reason: praise and criticism both distort judgment, so the team asks what they deeply believe about themselves ("are we actually innovating?") instead of what the world says.
- He writes before he creates anything. Daily practice: 15 minutes of nonstop free writing on his own free app, Freewrites (freewrites.io), which earns him nothing. He angles his mind toward work and story, and hooks and good sentences appear.
- Advice he gave his YC batch: open Instagram Reels, record 30 unedited seconds on what you're doing, post, and repeat for 30 days. Nobody did it, and instead founders hired agencies for $10M-announcement videos "nobody cares [about] in two days."
- His reasoning: across 30 videos, one will probably hit about 1,000 views while others get about 50. Ask why, then make the next 30 better. "First make a thousand bad videos, or at least 30 bad videos over 30 days." His own instinct comes from having made thousands of bad ones.
- On people wanting the "big flashy DSLR presence": "Everybody wants to make the Odyssey before they've even made a shitty iPhone movie."

chunks.heading: Public persona and what he shares
chunks.text:
- He says he doesn't think about comparisons to Steve Jobs and is "so far from being that level."
- He struggles to name living founders who inspire them the way Patrick Collison and Brian Chesky did in 2018; much of the industry conversation today is hate toward figures like Sam Altman or the Anthropic founders.
- His philosophy: share only what you're building and your take on what the world needs. Nobody knows his politics or personal life, only his products. He thinks that is the best form of communication, preferable to "random CEO pulling up to CNN talking about his take of the future."
- He has kept a Pakistani flag on his Twitter profile for about a decade, because growing up he never saw anyone who looked like him building technology. He wanted to be someone his younger self, "a Pakistani kid from Florida," could have looked up to.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains how Buildspace pivoted from homeschool software to a free school for builders by following what excited him rather than a problem statement. He covers culture as the moat, hyper-specific audiences, being particular about every word, separating emotions from metrics, and raising money by letting investors come to you.

chunks.heading: Building the Hogwarts for builders: Farza's path to buildspace
chunks.text:
**Background and early companies**
- Farza started his first business at 13 after his dad refused to let him take a job spinning a sign outside a gym.
- He found a bag of his parents' donation clothes, sold a Polo Ralph Lauren shirt on eBay for about $9, and lost about $10 to fees and shipping.
- He kept going. Within two years it was a business doing roughly $120-130k a year in revenue at about 70% margin, which he describes as shipping up to 40 packages a day.
- He made almost two YouTube videos a week for four years (500+ videos), and credits that volume for his speaking and writing ability.
- He did a computer science degree at a "bottom two" university (UCF) because it was easy and left time to build. He did it mainly to satisfy his mom.

**What buildspace is and how it works**
- Farza describes buildspace as "a school for people who don't want to get a job."
- It has two majors, Web3 and machine learning. To finish a piece of content you must build and ship something to real people, not just study the math.
- Next comes "nights and weekends", a six-week sprint where people take what they learned and ship their own idea. The idea can be venture scale, for their neighborhood, or just for fun.
- Examples he gives: people going from zero to a job or a $2M raise in six weeks, and a musician trying to grow from 400 to 4,000 Spotify monthly listeners.
- The goal is not a job or a fundraise. It is to help people figure out what excites them and make progress on it.
- He contrasts this with bootcamps: "I'm not sitting here trying to teach you JavaScript... I don't give a [ __ ] about JavaScript." Skills are a means to an end.
- It is free for everyone. He says charging $10,000 would shut out "that random Pakistani kid" while meaning nothing to a Google PM.
- He says the content is "nothing special", about 12 pieces on a website. The differentiator is culture, the way Nike or Stanford sell culture more than product.

**Building culture from day zero**
- Every decision gets the question: "why is it different, why does it feel different?"
- He kicked off each cohort with a live Twitch show to rally people, "like Goku bringing the Spirit Bomb together."
- At the start he ran these three times a week (Saturday and two on Sunday), and says buildspace's growth came largely from him standing in front of thousands of people each week.
- He is introverted, so being on camera suits him better than meeting people in person.
- He says skills come from reps. He got good at speaking and writing by making things he enjoyed, not by trying to get good at speaking, and you need to stick with a skill for over a year before you can judge it.

**Brand, voice and growth tactics**
- The first 1,000 users came from "infiltrating" CS clubs at about 20 schools. The team built each a landing page (buildspace.so/<school>) and sent it to students.
- Pitch: "we're bringing the builders together at Berkeley, are you in?" It was backed by YC and a16z, so students wanted in. Schools gave about 20 users on average and some gave 200.
- He insists on being hyper-specific about the audience, e.g. 18-22 year olds at US colleges who want internships. If you can't describe your user three levels deep, you can't market to them. You can assume the details at the start.
- He is very selective about where buildspace is mentioned. He does almost no interviews, magazines or blogs, because any mention of the name should be somewhere really cool and he doesn't want his message mangled.
- Early on he delivered the message himself on Twitch and Twitter, which he calls very targeted.
- He polices voice in detail: lowercase, friendly support replies, not corporate ("why did you reply as if you work at Google?"). Tweets are never more than two lines in a row, and he checks how a tweet looks on mobile versus desktop.
- He admits the balance: spend some time on polish, but the growth engine matters too.

**Pivoting and choosing what to build**
- The company started in December 2019 as Zip Homeschool, software that registered a homeschool per state's laws. He built it in about two days.
- By the time of YC, with about 50 customers and then 40 in month four, he pivoted. He had also seen users abusing the homeschool system.
- Next came Zip School, a live TV channel for kids. It reached roughly 30,000 monthly users and millions of streamed minutes a week with a small team and about five teachers. It raised $2.2M from a16z around demo day in summer 2020.
- Over the following year he pivoted repeatedly: virtual classes with real teachers (about 50 part-time teachers), a mobile game, a "MasterClass for kids" and async recorded courses. He counts about 10 pivots total.
- By August 2021 he was out of ideas. Parents only paid for math and reading, which he didn't care about. He decided on a market pivot to developers.
- He wrote four content ideas (self-driving cars, machine learning, Web3, gaming), posted on Twitter, and got about 100 signups. Web3 had the most, so that is what he built.
- He tells his team: "trust me for two weeks." Results showed in two weeks and kept showing every two weeks after.
- He is wary of market pivots; the Zip Homeschool to Zip School move was only a product pivot with the same K-5 audience for about a year and a half.
- Idea advice: follow what you find interesting and ask "wouldn't it be sick though?" Don't let "what problem does it solve?" dictate the start, because it can't fire you up for 10 years. Time-box it to about six weeks, then check whether it solves a real problem. Don't let startup media or essays act as absolute laws. Airbnb or Stripe doing something doesn't mean you must.
- After six weeks, thousands of people had gone through buildspace. They said they hated college or their job and that it showed them a different path, which became the problem it solved.

**Metrics, mindset and sustaining the long game**
- Keep the graph in front of you, but if it's down, don't feel bad. Analyze what happened and change what you're doing: "if it's not growing, it doesn't mean you suck, it just means what you're doing sucks."
- Blaming himself sped up his learning, but he says it isn't sustainable over years.
- He aims to be about 90% logical and 10% emotionally attached, and if he drifts to 70/30 he takes a day.
- Don't emulate people. He copied Jeff Bezos as a teen and says it leaves you a "hodgepodge" of others. He warns against chasing a billion-dollar company as a goal, since that exhausts you.
- Expect it to take three to six years to get good at this, and accept that family and friends may doubt you.

**Fundraising: $10M at a $100M valuation**
- He says he has never sent a cold email to raise money. His approach is to create value, tell the world, and let investors come.
- a16z reached out when he had about 800-1,000 Twitter followers, which led to the $2.2M round about three months later.
- For the $10M round, he says winning a16z first meant the rest followed. Investors also included Founders Inc, Gary Vee and others.
- Having thousands of people going through the product each week made it far easier. He called it an intense month and a half.
- His advice: "build your network before you need it." The best network is a product people love, so ask how to get the right people to come to you.

**Context he gives on the team and current stage**
- At the time of the interview he describes buildspace as a small team that is profitable via sponsorships, and says he is serious about building a big company.
- He says his current "mountain" is balancing his drive to build with relationships, and that being a "degenerate" grinder works at 20-25 but not at 27.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza (Buildspace, Hey Clicky) explains how he picks ideas by their one-line hook, thinks about the story while building, and gets first customers through real people before social media. He argues for charging from day one, judging inputs over outputs, and treating daily posting as a lottery ticket.

chunks.heading: Start with the one-line hook before writing code
chunks.text:
- Farza says he does not write a line of code until he has a headline-style line for the product. For Hey Clicky it was "An AI that can see your screen and teach you anything." His test: would he stop scrolling if he read it as an Instagram, TikTok or Twitter headline?
- He thinks of the Instagram caption while building, and compares it to writing a song where melody and lyrics come together. Before shipping a new feature he already asks how he will announce it the next day.
- He borrows from Miyazaki, who won't start a film until he has the first frame. Everyone then works around that frame, which sets the art style, story and character. For software, Farza says the "first frame" is often the first 5 seconds of the demo or the one-line caption.
- He keeps a notes app full of candidate lines and picks the ones that excite him. He did not know Clicky would be the winner when he wrote its line.
- He is baffled by founders who ask how to get their first 1,000 customers after they have built the product. Distribution "should be the first thing you think about."
- He says he doesn't care about marketing or acquisition as concepts. He needs the messaging to be good so that he stays a fan of his own product, and he calls himself his own worst critic on it.
- Current example: users rarely use Clicky's agent, but those who do like it. That led to the idea of running the agent without being asked, and the line "The world's first proactive agent."

chunks.heading: Building in public with a tiny audience: consistency over followers
chunks.text:
- Farza rejects the claim that his products only work because he has a big following. If the product is bad, a huge audience won't help: a famous director or a celebrity with a poor product still gets ignored.
- He says today's algorithms are better than ever, and few people create content consistently. His claim: starting from zero, you are maybe 30 to 60 posts from 10,000 followers, then 50,000.
- His 2019 story: he was building an online school for kids with about 25 LinkedIn connections and about 50 Twitter followers. He posted progress on Twitter twice a day and on Substack weekly. After about 6 months a partner at A16Z, who had followed the progress, invested $2 million while Farza had around 600 followers.
- He says he is "a nobody from Florida" and an outsider. His view is that outsiders are "200 days of consistency away" from changing their situation, but most people quit around day 45 with five views.
- He quotes Mr. Beast's idea of not talking until you've made 2,000 videos. He applies the same logic to software: you probably need 1,000 to 2,000 launches before something hits.

chunks.heading: Measure inputs, not outputs
chunks.text:
- His rule is to focus on inputs. A made video counts, and views don't matter to him: "I made the video. Full stop."
- He uses a basketball analogy. Judging yourself on every missed shot is crazy when you take hundreds a day, yet makes still matter, so you measure on a cadence.
- Company-level check: every 2 weeks he steps back and looks at the numbers analytically, not emotionally. For example, going from zero views one week to 10 the next counts as progress.
- Elite players, he says, review their stats and replays roughly monthly and track how often they practice. He sees the same pattern in building: show up, ship, review periodically.
- He admits people prefer results (the shot going in, the championship, money) because inputs are a harder thing to be motivated by. Unless you hit the lottery, those results take a long time.

chunks.heading: Getting your first 10 customers: talk to real people, skip social media
chunks.text:
- When people ask how to talk about their product online, he first asks why they need to. His first instinct is to call friends and talk to 10 people in real life.
- For a hypothetical crypto wallet for teenagers, he would ask teens and parents directly. He lists places to find them: high school PTA meetings, grocery stores, farmers markets.
- He thinks a founder in 2026 might be best off deleting social accounts and not posting until they have their first 10 customers. Many people make 10 TikToks or 50 Reels, get about 20 downloads, burn out and quit. He says social media is distracting and defeating for founders because it makes you feel behind. He has said he would not use it until about 50 to 100 customers.
- His first Hey Clicky conversation was with his friend Joshua, a video editor with 10 to 20 years of experience. Joshua asked if it could do a specific color-grading technique. It could, and that led to new ideas.
- For the 2020 YC interview for his online elementary school, Zip School, he had his mom and dad interview him about the idea for about 6 minutes a day. They knew nothing about YC. When they said they didn't understand, that signaled the pitch was too complicated.
- When picking an idea in a category (like the Gemini X Prize categories), he asks what he can build in a day and give to someone. He builds a small version, gives it to his mom or the friend across the street, and sees whether they love or hate it.

chunks.heading: When and how to post online
chunks.text:
- Once you are past roughly 10 customers and heading toward 100, he would start making videos online, about two to three a day.
- If you want to start right now, his lowest-effort, highest-reward advice is to pull out your phone and make three talking-to-camera videos today and post them.
- Example script: "My name is Farza. I'm working on this crypto wallet for teenagers. If you're a parent of a teenager, drop a comment, I'd love to talk to you." He says that might get him two parents to talk to.
- Posting daily is "like playing the lottery" for free. Don't expect virality by video 10; it is more likely to be around the 200th.
- If a founder's mental state suffers, he says skip it. He thinks filming 30 seconds a day is less daunting than building the product.
- Faceless formats work. A friend's workout app reached $3 million a year in revenue on a $10 a month plan, and his entire TikTok was AI-generated anime characters working out with the app, with no face or voice. He later got in trouble over using the characters, but Farza says it no longer mattered. His take: "I ask for forgiveness, not permission."

chunks.heading: Charge money from day one
chunks.text:
- Farza's view is that the best way to learn whether people will pay is to charge. He says most people building today should charge from day one and skip the free plan.
- Early on he sees a free plan as useless and noisy. He thinks a free plan only becomes interesting once you pass about 10,000 users.
- He advises pre-orders even when the product isn't ready, and refunding if you don't deliver. He gave this advice to a founder with a waitlist for a device that helps people sleep better.
- The pitch should force a clear answer: "Cost 20 bucks a month. Are you in or are you out?" A "no" is valuable because the person tells you why.
- Hey Clicky has a $20 a month plan and a $100 a month plan. He added a free plan only as it grew. For the first 100 users he says paying users are far higher signal.

chunks.heading: Reading signals and learning from early users
chunks.text:
- His rule for building: make the thing and give it to at least one person, who must use it or pay for it. That is when it becomes real.
- In 2025 he started a new idea roughly every 3 days, probably 20 or more, and ran out of people who cared. He calls this exhausting and says it is not the romantic version people imagine.
- His signal for committing to an idea is whether it inspires more ideas on the same idea, so that you build "like a skyscraper" and it compounds.
- Clicky data points: after going viral it got about 8,000 downloads, and about 400 users stuck around for 5 straight days. He says virality alone means nothing; retention is what blew his mind.
- He called those retained users one by one: kids, teachers, students and programmers. One was a 55-year-old woman using it to get copywriting feedback on her Shopify cookie store. She is not a native English speaker and found Shopify's AI features poor.
- He says the point of talking to customers is to spark your own ideas. If one user loves the agent and another never uses it, he asks how to make it useful to the second user using the first user's pattern. Find the people who get it and take what excites them to others.
- Example: one user loved it for DaVinci Resolve, so he built a marketing routine and Instagram Reels around video editors.
- He initially open-sourced Hey Clicky, expecting no one to care, then closed future work after 2 days when interest was high. The original code stays public.
- He argues you never "hit the lottery" with a company. Like a rapper who can't release the same song weekly, you must keep shipping the next thing. He sees every day and week as a new launch, and tries to put things out as quickly as possible.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains why he shut down Buildspace instead of selling it, the 6 months of doing nothing that followed, and how he rebuilt momentum by shipping something every week. Covers how he picks collaborators and hires, how HeyClicky grew out of a throwaway side project, and how he thinks about money and happiness.

chunks.heading: Farza on shutting down Buildspace: timing, selling, and the team
chunks.text:
- Farza thought about shutting down Buildspace for about a year before doing it. He talked it over with a friend a year before S5 IRL and gave the company 6 to 12 months to see if the feeling held: "you can't just shut down four years of work in like a couple of days."
- The decision point was after the S5 kickoff. His diary says S5 reached about 130,000 people, and the kickoff stream had about 20,000 live. He thought: "this is like the best it's ever going to be technically. Great team, great environment, everything's working", and he still didn't want to do it.
- His reasoning: "It's hard to run a company, but it's even harder to fake running a company." A good team sees through a founder who is no longer in it, so staying would have been a disservice to the team, fans and product.
- He ran S5 IRL fully anyway. His feeling in the moment was "this must all get done properly" and "we must not let the people down". The emotional crash came after the final post went out.
- He says he cares about the reputation of the roughly 20 people who worked at the company over 5 years more than his own. He wanted "worked at Buildspace" to stay a good line on a CV, not a stain.
- Public reaction was far better than he feared. Almost no one turned on him, and fans he met while traveling said versions of "I'm not happy about it but I get why you did it."

chunks.heading: Farza on why he didn't sell Buildspace, and what he would change
chunks.text:
- Farza says the main reason he didn't sell was his own mindset: "I just thought the thing was worthless... why would anyone want this pile of garbage?" He admits this was wrong in hindsight, given the company's roughly $100M valuation.
- He says founders are "lost in the sauce" and can't see what the company is worth. He was always trying to push it forward, so he saw the flaws.
- He did look at selling and at hiring a CEO but didn't pursue them. There was no obvious acquirer or buyer for the IP. The ideas he had were non-obvious, such as Microsoft for Startups picking the company up for something like $25M.
- With no obvious option and a belief that the company had no value, he chose to close it out.
- The one thing he'd do differently: put much more effort into placing the team. He assumed no one on the team would want a job and felt it would be disrespectful to bring it up, so people had to fend for themselves. He says "I could have done a lot better there." Several of them ended up at Founders Inc., which he credits to luck, not his effort.
