- He also thinks the company could have found a different home, with some financial moves done differently. He had "no regrets" overall.

chunks.heading: Farza on the 6 months of doing nothing after Buildspace
chunks.text:
- After closing Buildspace, Farza took 6 months fully offline and traveled. A friend in Amsterdam told him to go to a different city every week and ask locals where to go next. He bounced between countries, including Berlin, Morocco and Pakistan.
- The first 3 months were bad. After 10 years on a laptop he felt dazed and didn't know what to do with himself.
- He wanted to prove to himself he had no compulsive "itch" to build. He did: he could sit on a couch all day and be happy.
- He found he didn't know whether he was happy, because he'd been wired only to make the company work. He asked an AI to scan his diary entries for the last time he was happy, and the answer was close to "pretty much nothing."
- His fix was a notebook where he rated each day out of 10 for happiness. For the first weeks he wrote "? out of 10." Eventually he logged days as a 6 and kept auditing what made him unhappy.
- He questioned habits that were really performance fuel, not enjoyment: running 10 km a day, watching anime, sauna and cold plunge. He found he liked simpler things, like grocery shopping and cooking, which he'd never done because he'd used DoorDash for 6 years.
- He spent hours a day in quiet churches and mosques as a way to be calm.
- He came back to San Francisco when he felt he could "reliably wake up and just be happy." His reason was only a gut feeling that something good was waiting there.
- On "optimize for impact, not happiness": he won't prescribe it for others, but he doesn't think he'll build anything good by being consistently unhappy. He says it isn't a playground, and "there are weeks or months that are hard," but he avoids being unhappy daily.

chunks.heading: Farza on rebuilding after a public failure: shots, collaboration and the comeback frame
chunks.text:
- At his lowest, Farza believed no one would ever want to work with him or hear his name again. He says kind words from friends didn't change his mental state; only doing things did.
- His comeback frame came from people he admires, such as Steve Jobs with NeXT, Elon, Porter Robinson and LeBron. All had a stretch of public embarrassment or a lost championship before the next win. He compares himself to a good player who got injured in the playoffs, not a bad player.
- He defines "winning the championship" as doing the height of his work every day, consistently, while happy and energized. In business terms it means building something that wouldn't exist without him and his team together, like an iPhone or a Tesla.
- His 2025 approach was to take shots like a basketball player: sit on the court and shoot daily. His rule was "I have to make something and show at least one person" every week. He made something new almost daily, including a Slack interface for AI agents, a VR game about battling gorillas, a journaling tool called Free Write, and an AI tutorial channel.
- On bad ideas: "I don't care if it's horrible." He treats output as a muscle, and says nobody can name a single thing he did in 2025, but he needed that year to get where he is.
- He found he was happiest making things with others and unhappiest alone. His early collaboration was low-pressure, such as a 2-week trip to Japan with a friend (Sharief) just to make things, which he called the most healing creative activity of the previous two years.
- When a side project with a friend faded after 3 months, they both simply said they didn't want to keep going, so it never became a company. Timing and mindset have to match for both people.

chunks.heading: Farza on hiring and picking collaborators
chunks.text:
- His top filter is whether he enjoys talking to the person: "that's like 95%." The last 5% is that they are really good at their craft.
- He tests skill through conversation. A real expert on a topic shows it within about 30 seconds, from the questions asked and the opening thoughts on the subject.
- For AI hires he asks how quickly they try a new model when it comes out. He once worked with someone who always did it within 5 minutes, and who dropped everything to tell him what had changed.
- He has interviewed somewhere between 1,000 and 2,000 people. To hire one person he figures he interviews around 80 to 100.
- He prefers to work with candidates for 2 to 3 months before hiring, ideally with them in person. If the company would fall apart when they leave after 3 months, that was the right person: "I'll do everything to keep that person."
- He prefers people he has history with, because he knows how they react when things go badly. His new team includes Nish, who won Buildspace Nights and Weekends season one and joined about two weeks before this recording.

chunks.heading: Farza on how HeyClicky started and the Clicky product path
chunks.text:
- Farza's 2026 shift was to pick one thing: AI. He had trained models since 2016. While traveling he noticed he knew far more about AI than the people around him, and he taught strangers (for example a surf-camp owner in Morocco, who built his first website with him in a day).
- His thesis was to "democratize the models." He compares models to the craziest chips in the world with no laptop built around them yet.
- The first step was the dumbest, most direct one: stream on YouTube and teach people AI, the way he would teach someone on the street. With Julian, he helped about 10,000 people in a single month, and about 5,000 of them made their first thing with AI. He didn't want to be a YouTuber long term and did it to learn.
- In the community he saw the sticking point: beginners don't know what to type in the first box of tools like Claude Code, Codex or Replit, or what to do after the first website. So he built a tool that watched the learner's screen and guided them step by step, which was the first version, called Learning Buddy.
- Clicky came from a moment while he was learning DaVinci Resolve (to color grade his own videos). He kept screenshotting it into Claude 20 times in a row, and realized his existing code could let a model see his screen and teach him in real time. If it could teach DaVinci, it could teach almost anything.
- He sat on the idea for two weeks, thinking it was "pretty nonsense." His YC partner Aaron told him to just post it. His mentality: "I don't care how dog the idea is. I will happily just post it because I have no care about my reputation."
- About 8 weeks after posting, it was a company with a team, a "beautiful product" and paying users.
- He joined YC after Aaron pushed him for a couple of weeks. The line that landed was "you're already building your house alone." He joined with his YouTube channel and was working on a different idea for about the first month.

chunks.heading: Farza on fundraising for HeyClicky and how HeyClicky differs from Buildspace
chunks.text:
- Farza says he fell into raising money, and each round came from relationships, not pitching:
  - About $300,000 from Founders Inc. (Ken) and Ryan Hoover, after he came back to SF and was nearly broke. He texted them to say he didn't know what he was doing but would build a company. His alternative was taking a job for a year at a large salary.
  - YC's $500,000.
  - $3 million from Ivan at Excel, whom he knew from his one job at 22 (training models at Mayhem, an AI gaming coach). Ivan offered it while Farza was still working on the YouTube channel.
- After YC demo day, his inbox was full of investors, and he says his content was getting millions of views. He lands at a $12 million total raise.
- He chose $12M on purpose: Buildspace raised $12M across its history (including Zip School), so he knew how to use that amount of capital. He liked putting himself in the same position again with a different company and team.
- He likes having more money "to an extent", since more capital lets him get more creative on the product and company.
- Biggest difference from Buildspace: he is now very focused on the business. He knows daily whether the company makes money and how much it loses per user, whereas at Buildspace the attitude was "we made a million there, we lost two million there, okay, next." He thinks he's a good business person but has never shown it, because he works in viral consumer products where building a great business is classically hard.
- The other difference is not "losing my head": setting up his own life so the earlier burnout doesn't recur.
- On success: he judges each day by whether it ended with a smiley face and good work shipped, and he aims to feel inspired at least once a day, because inspiration usually leads to good work. He says being "aloof" is partly a defense mechanism: if he took it too seriously, he'd psych himself out.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza Majeed (buildspace) tells his path from selling blank DVDs and clothes online to self-driving research to buildspace. He argues for committing to one endeavor so learnings compound, designing a tight viral core loop before writing code, and building distribution through content. Tech is only a tool for solving a problem.

chunks.heading: Start with something repeatable, and run the supplier playbook online
chunks.text:
- Farza started companies at 13 and says he had one near $100K in revenue by 15.
- His first sales were his dad's donated clothes on eBay, such as Calvin Klein jeans at about $10.
- That became a garage-sale flipping business, where he had to "make magic every single weekend" to find stock.
- He then sold blank DVDs to indie game developers in Latin America (around 2009), who needed discs to burn and sell their games.
- The idea came from his uncle's DVD shop. A local supplier sold blank discs and sleeves, so he did the same thing on the internet.
- His lesson is that a product he could recreate and repeat beat the one-off hustle of garage sales.
- He ran the DVD business for about seven years. It later pivoted into a t-shirt business and other things.

chunks.heading: Commit to one thing so learnings compound
chunks.text:
- He rejects the "new product every month" approach: "nothing will teach you more than just grinding on the same thing every day for like three years."
- A founder who launched six unrelated products probably "didn't learn anything," because learning comes from launching and then sitting on it.
- Pivoting is fine when the new thing is close to the old one, so the lessons carry over. He calls pivoting every two to three months into something unrelated "crazy."
- He sets basic numeric goals early and tracks them:
  - eBay: $100 in revenue.
  - Self-driving car: a target model accuracy.
  - Buildspace: a number by the end of the month or year.
- He warns against working for 10 years on something only five people use, unless that is genuinely what you want.
- He still gives himself this advice at 26 and frames the goal as being a happy builder.

chunks.heading: Build the core loop before writing code
chunks.text:
- Consumer products grow from a simple loop that you build once and then repeat.
- Buildspace's loop: sign up, enroll in a project, complete it, get an NFT, post it on Twitter, repeat. He credits this loop for essentially all of the early growth.
- He says to "draw that circle on a piece of paper before you write any code" and check that it makes sense.
- Making a React app is easy now. The impressive part is people using it the day after launch.
- Other growth levers he names:
  - Shipping something new every month, such as a new project each month, which got Buildspace onto Solana's homepage.
  - Partnering with blockchains and college blockchain clubs, which supplied the earliest users.
  - Being honest with the community.
- The first step was distribution: free web3 learning content that captured emails and an audience, which grew to about 55,000 Discord members.

chunks.heading: Talk to users and pivot early
chunks.text:
- Buildspace pivoted into web3 about two weeks after starting, because users said they wanted to learn web3.
- He already liked the tech, which made the pivot easy.
- Zip School (homeschooling) began as a Webflow form plus Typeform, built in a day or two at a hackathon.
- The first customer paid $10 a month, and he walked her through the process manually.
- About three months later it had roughly 50 customers and around $500 MRR, and he applied to YC.
- During YC he pivoted again, to "Twitch for kids" with about 30 teachers streaming, and raised from a16z on that.
- He values having a few people ahead of him to ask dumb questions. One was a friend who is now Thirdweb's CEO and gave him $25K early. He calls YC a school for founders who ask dumb questions.
- For him YC was an easy call: he was a solo founder with no money, and his YC partners helped through real problems.

chunks.heading: Turn a content audience into a network with ownership
chunks.text:
- Content was the way in. The long-term goal is a network, closer to LinkedIn, where professionals connect.
- Claimed metrics at the time:
  - About 20,000 profiles, growing around 5,000 every couple of days.
  - Hundreds of companies using the recruiting tool.
  - Inbound hiring requests from companies like Disney, who "just want to be where the most activity is."
  - About $1M in revenue.
- His view of the moat in big social networks is that people stay only because the network is there. Buildspace can undercut that by rewarding core actions with ownership:
  - Learning something, referring five people, or connecting with ten people each earns an NFT.
  - Part of revenue goes into a public treasury governed by NFT holders.
  - Holders can fund sub-groups such as Buildspace India, Women, Africa and Founders.
- On tokenized communities, he rejects a liquid, speculative coin because it fills the community with people trying to make money.
- He prefers non-transferable, non-liquid NFTs given for good contributions, which give people a seat at the table on what comes next.

chunks.heading: Monetization and planning horizon
chunks.text:
- Normal users stay free. He doesn't plan to charge regular end users.
- Protocols such as Solana, Polygon, Ethereum and Avalanche pay Buildspace for access to its community.
- He sees a possible premium model for larger companies, built around the recruiting tool, but says the exact model isn't set.
- He plans on three horizons: one month, one year and ten years. The 10-year vision can stay vague ("a product used by billions") because the details will change.
- He thinks planning month by month for years is pointless.

chunks.heading: Treat technology as a tool
chunks.text:
- He tinkers with emerging tech (AR, ML, web3, brain hardware) and does biweekly "hack days" with friends, shipping something in a day.
- His advice: "Don't get too captured by technologies." Machine learning or web3 has no value on its own, only through the problem it solves.
- He compares the rush into web3 to the rush into ML in 2016, and says people who chase hype should ask what problem they push forward.
- He sees body and brain hardware as the next shift: EEG headsets, finger-tracking gloves and eye-tracking cameras.
- He thinks starting with this hardware costs little. Buildspace's treasury funded a 16-year-old for about $300 for a disability-related project.

chunks.heading: Team and hiring
chunks.text:
- Buildspace is mostly remote, at seven people and heading to 12 or 13.
- He says to meet teammates in person early and keep meeting every quarter or so, because going from in-person to remote is easy and the reverse is hard.
- He doesn't care about age and hired a 16-year-old.
- He says he'd rather pay someone to build something they pitch than run an "internship."
- On college he says "useless 99 percent of the time." He attended only to make his mom happy, and thinks you can build the same social experience for far less.
- A smaller, tight community of 10,000 who care beats 50,000 in a Discord, since closeness dilutes with scale.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza (Hey Clicky, Buildspace) explains why launching in 2026 means posting raw demos constantly on algorithmic platforms instead of one polished launch. He covers scripting hooks, tracking conversion per channel, targeting small niche audiences, and hiring a filmmaker early.

chunks.heading: Make the video a mini demo, not a polished launch
chunks.text:
- Farza treats "launching" as a continuous channel, not a one-time event. In his words: "We're not launching to like get a bunch of clout on the internet." The goal is users, so he builds a repeatable channel.
- He calls these "demos" rather than launches and ships them constantly. The team asks "what are we launching this week?" and works backwards from the launch.
- For each feature, the team decides the Instagram caption, the hook and the video angle before building it. As he puts it, "how we communicate to other people is just as important as what we're building."
- He says a video of him saying hi and describing the product can outperform a $20,000 produced video, because old media no longer matters.
- Polished launches happen only about once a quarter. Otherwise the cadence is near-daily raw demos.
- The raw "yo, check this out" feeling between co-founders is, in his view, exactly how to present yourself online.

chunks.heading: Judge success by retained users, not views
chunks.text:
- The first Clicky video got nearly 3 million views on Twitter. Farza said he does not care about the traffic and asks how many people actually downloaded and stayed.
- About 7,000 people downloaded Clicky after that video. Roughly 100 of them used it every day for 5 days straight.
- He contacted those ~100 users individually. They were using it in ways he never imagined, and that is what made him commit to building the company.
- He recorded that video in the office 5 minutes before dinner and almost didn't post it because he thought it wasn't good enough. It started as a side project he had open sourced.
- His rule: he is happy to post even if it gets zero views, and he forgets it by the time he clicks post, checking back about a week later.

chunks.heading: Script every video and write the hook for yourself
chunks.text:
- Farza scripts every video, including ones that look off the cuff, writing the script about 3 days ahead. He rehearses lines in his head (shower, commute), so by the time the camera is on he has "visualized it like 10 times."
- Test for a script: "Do I enjoy reading this? Would I read this if someone texted this to me?"
- Test for a tweet: paste your text into a random tweet and ask whether your own eyes stop on it. If you wouldn't stop, don't post it. He applies this to Twitter, Instagram and YouTube.
- Structure: treat a 1-minute video like a movie, with a setup of only about 10-20%. The first 10 seconds should say what you're doing and why it matters.
- Formula he repeats: "This is who I am. This is what's going on. This is what I'm working on. Let me show you."
- Build for yourself. Frame the problem as his own ("when I'm writing, I often don't know what I want to say"), not "everyone has this problem." If he finds it cool, he assumes at least one other person will.
- Show your face clearly and be proud of who you are.
- Example hook: "Last week I went super viral for something I built that I thought was kind of ridiculous... and now I'm in Y Combinator." It targets the YC curiosity niche.

chunks.heading: Design the first frame and keep the story moving
chunks.text:
- The first frame of the Clicky video was deliberately Xcode, zoomed in on a tiny triangle, aimed at curious developers rather than video editors. Most people only see the first 3 seconds while scrolling.
- Constantly ask "Am I bouncing? When?" while watching content. Farza studies Instagram Reels to take notes on templates, such as a dark background and a caption like "2 months ago..." that creates curiosity.
- He uses "beats" in the voice-controlled computer demo: "No hands," the song plays, volume lowered by voice, then the Stripe dashboard opens so viewers wonder how much money he made. That video had no cuts.
- Result: 3.8M views on Twitter and 4.6M on Instagram.
- He aims to keep the story moving ("Where's this guy going? Come on") rather than trying to hold attention.
- Some videos are built for people with no attention span, such as "It has been 9 weeks since I built and launched my idea to the world." He mentally checks "Am I still watching?" at each beat.
- Everyone wants a story, so a demo should be a mini story. Viewers see him as a character, with the "Farza" in the video being a version of himself.

chunks.heading: Show your process: the weekly "everything we built this week" video
chunks.text:
- The team films a short update, made in about 10 minutes, where each person says what they shipped. These began as a way to stay accountable and now run every two weeks. One got nearly 1M views on Instagram.
- It has no hook or story, only the team telling what they did.
- His reasoning: what happens day to day inside a company is far from what outsiders imagine, and an inside look excites early adopters who wonder who the small team behind an AI product is.
- He is "anti" content about being a founder ("my day as a YC founder"). He shows what the team is doing and why, not his life.
- The tone is joyful, with music and the team clapping for each other.
- Practical tip: ask "what's something I did today that made me smile or felt new?", talk about it, show it, post, and go back to work.

chunks.heading: Pick channels by conversion, and target niches on every platform
chunks.text:
- Farza says users of any product are on algorithmic platforms (X, LinkedIn, TikTok, Instagram, YouTube), whether the product is drones, AI or a dating app.
- Targeted example: Clicky found three design agencies naturally, so he made TikToks addressed to them ("Are you the founder of a design agency? Stop right there"). That produced about 50 design agency leads. The videos averaged about 4,000 views each, all targeted. His goal is the right audience, not virality.
- Conversion by channel:
  - Twitter: worst conversion. The original Clicky video had 3M views and 7,000 downloads (under 1%). The 2.9M-view screen-aware dictation video converted horribly.
  - YouTube: a 20,000-view video converted about 20% to app downloads. The channel is brand new with 872 subscribers, and a video keeps working for years ("a library that will last for decades"). Twitter is "your moment once and you're gone."
  - Instagram: about 70% of Clicky's traffic, and by far the best channel for his audience.
- He tracks it with a bio link of "/ig", which lets him measure the conversion rate of Instagram visitors who download the app (including a button to send the link to themselves by email).
- Format: Instagram is vertical and Twitter prefers 16:9, so he makes videos for one platform and cross-posts. A drawing-on-screen demo made for Twitter performed even better on Instagram.
- One Instagram video has 21M views and still drives traffic. He now runs it as a Facebook ad.

chunks.heading: Volume, early reps and the team and gear behind it
chunks.text:
- His old ZipSchool launch video got 23 likes, one bookmark and one comment, and he still counts it as a launch. The day-one launch was just a landing page with no copy and a Canva video, to about 80 followers.
- Over years he kept posting, like basketball: "If you don't take a thousand shots, you're not going to make the 5,000th shot." In his words, "In order to not be cringe, you must first be cringe."
- First hires: a filmmaker and an engineer. Videos are made by Vikrant, who helps with shots, hooks, sets and editing. Farza brings the script, the song and the vibe.
- At one point Clicky had three people making videos and one engineer. Code is easy to clone now, but the audience, community and energy around a product are not.
- Stack:
  - Screen Studio (about $30) for screen demos.
  - iPhone selfie camera, edited in Instagram's Edits app.
  - Sony FX3 with a DJI mic for more cinematic videos.
  - DaVinci for laptop editing.
  - Freewrite (freewrite.io, his free open source app) for writing the script.
- Audio is the most important thing: "If your audio is bad, I'm bouncing." Use any mic that isn't the MacBook or AirPods mic; a cheap used DJI mic is enough.
- Solo founders should start with the phone.

chunks.heading: The 30-day challenge
chunks.text:
- Spend 10 minutes a day recording yourself on your phone talking about what you did that day. Post it on Instagram or TikTok, on a new account if you want.
- Do this for 30 days straight. He promises at least one will pass 1,000 views, and you then base the next video on that one.
- Only about 1-2% of people he advises to do this actually do it, because they fear looking stupid. He says it is never easier to get your message out.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains how Buildspace evolved from web3 tutorials into Nights & Weekends and a physical school by following its most motivated users. He covers selling a story instead of a community, building for shy beginners, hiring by conversation, and running a team with trust and no task board.

chunks.heading: Farza's path into building: eBay, film school, and learning to "just do the work"
chunks.text:
- At 13 he took a gym sign-spinner job. His dad (a car-sales/finance guy) told him he could be more than that, and Farza says his dad always "train[ed] me to think entrepreneurially."
- He then started selling donated clothes on eBay, and later a very specific type of blank DVD from one supplier.
- He says he was "the main guy on the market" for that product because he offered discount codes and did things other eBay sellers wouldn't, since at 15-16 he didn't know the rules.
- His margins were about 5%, he describes the money as good, and the business (Clothing House) passed $100K in sales before he was 18.
- He only went to college (UCF) because his mom wanted him to. His view: "the only valid reason" to finish school is a family promise like that.
- He argues the main bad reason to go is wanting "a place to figure it out", and he asks whether you can't gather 10 people like you and work together instead.
- At 18 his alternative plan was a house in South Florida with about 10 people who were also selling on eBay and making things online.
- He started in the film program (he wanted to be like Christopher Nolan). He left after seeing that film students watched movies while computer science students were "doing stuff from day one", so he switched to CS to make things immediately.
- His mindset: do everything as well as he can, and treat existing narratives as challenges to route around.

chunks.heading: Why he thinks college is "broken": expectations, not the education
chunks.text:
- Farza says college in its purest form is good: "you go there and you learn something new and you leave", you learn to learn.
- What's broken is the promise that a degree gets you a job or a guaranteed income. He blames "whoever created that narrative", not the student.
- He frames Buildspace as "just a different path from college", a space to figure out your own idea, and not only for 18-year-olds. A 50-year-old with an idea can do it too.
- He says going to a weaker school (UCF, ranked around 180 at the time) helped him: he was surrounded by "normal people", not "killers", which let him build confidence.
- He suspects MIT or Berkeley would have drained that confidence. He arrived in San Francisco extremely confident.
- He says digital relationships can go far: his best friend is someone he has met in person about six times, from a Battlefield 3 ranking. Online can come first, and people over-index on physical proximity.
- Founders Inc began digitally as Furqan's weekly Discord chat during Covid, where he gave away one Ethereum (about $500 then) each week. The physical space came later.

chunks.heading: How Nights & Weekends emerged from tutorials
chunks.text:
- Buildspace started as web3 tutorials (the Dowel course is cited as a hit). The tutorials "only got so big" and then fizzled, and he had no clear next step.
- He talked to users, who all said they wanted to keep working on their projects. People were customizing the tutorial projects (full DAOs came from a simple tutorial), which showed him demand for more depth.
- So he created a six-week program as a side project inside a roughly 5-6 person company. It wasn't an accelerator, just six weeks to take your project further.
- He pitched it to Stefan, who helped name it Nights & Weekends and design the brand. They shipped it fast.
- Season 1 numbers: 450 people started, about 60 graduated, and 40 bought tickets to come to San Francisco. The in-person event was only planned a week or two before.
- Seasons grew to about 1,200 (season 2), 7,500 (season 3) and 17,000 (season 4). He thought season 2 would break at 1,200, but it worked the same way at larger numbers.
- Early positioning was literally "a place for the hackers and the painters" (a Paul Graham line).
- Season 1 and 2 focused on web3 and AI. By season 3 he "opened up the gates" to artists, painters and other makers.
- His habit: every season he asks the team for "10 reasons we don't kill Nights & Weekends." He gets bored fast, but doesn't quit when bored. He asks "what needs to change here?" and kills the product only if nothing does.

chunks.heading: Building a one-to-many story, not a "community"
chunks.text:
- Farza grew up watching Twitch streams and was struck by how close he felt to a streamer despite thousands in chat. That is why Buildspace is one-to-many.
- His premise: tell a great story and people will want to be part of it and complete their arc in it.
- He says "I even hate the word community". In his view Buildspace has a story that people attach to, more than to him personally.
- His comparison: "Harry Potter is a story." Readers feel like Ron or Harry. The team's job is to keep writing the next chapters and not let anyone else write the book, while leaving room for people to insert themselves.
- Concrete tactics: thousands watching together, funny videos, colorful image drops people become attached to, and "shenanigans".
- Buildspace never called itself a course or a cohort. The pitch was "come join us and work on your idea" with no expectation.
- He defines cringe from his gamer and film background: ugly shots, bad audio, and forcing 12 people into a group call. He is shy himself, so he optimizes for introverts (sit alone eight hours a day and share updates), assuming everyone is shy like him.
- He argues the world builds for people already confident and ambitious. Accelerators ignore you if you aren't building something big. Buildspace welcomes a small album or a to-do list app the same as a billion-dollar company.
- Word of mouth ("that Farza guy" / "that Buildspace thing") is the main way people find it, plus him being public about the journey on Twitter.
- Cringe for him changes over time. They called it Hogwarts for a while, then moved away from that branding.
- He controls the narrative, which is why he avoids magazines and business articles.

chunks.heading: Moving from online to a physical school
chunks.text:
- Users who finished Nights & Weekends wanted more, and Farza had "nothing for them", yet they were his most motivated audience.
- His reasoning: the best version of Buildspace puts great people in front of you helping and teaching in person, not over a call. He made it for himself ("I would have never gone to a virtual school").
- About six months before this interview he decided to open a physical campus, spend as little as possible, and ship a Lo-Fi MVP.
- They spent about three months on it. He sketched the designs in his notebook and found two designers (Issa and Kyle) from Twitter.
- He threw a pizza party at the Founders Inc space and invited anyone to come look and give ideas. About 50 people showed up, and he found the two designers by talking to people for a few minutes.
- He wants a school to feel like McDonald's: Stanford's best parts delivered at McDonald's-style scale and consistency. He says that if they can keep quality at scale "we'll be number one", and otherwise "we'll probably flop."
- He doesn't run the campus day to day (Ahmed does). He says the brand can last as long as he does, and he compares it to Steve Jobs fronting Apple for 40 years.
- Ten-year picture: hundreds of thousands of people online through Nights & Weekends worldwide, thousands graduating through physical campuses, ideally about 25 campuses.
- Campus locations come from places the team likes to visit (for example Dubai "because we went to Dubai and it was fun"). He wants to pick by following the team's hearts but being logical about it and not getting emotionally attached.

chunks.heading: Funding, monetization and the business model
chunks.text:
- He raised $10M from a16z while the product was still the web3 tutorials. His pitch to every investor: "you're not giving the idea $10 million, you're giving me $10 million", so vet him as much as you like.
- His original idea for the tutorials was teaching many people, helping them start companies or get jobs, and possibly tokenizing it.
- On monetization he says education has few models that get big. The one they're testing: charge governments a subscription to run a campus in their city.
- Example given: Abu Dhabi paying about $2M a year for a campus expected to produce a set amount of new revenue, companies and jobs.
- His angle is that most people in the program (musicians, YouTubers, small business owners) are essentially small companies, and governments want more innovators in their towns.
- He says this path could make Buildspace the biggest education company, and he was heading to Dubai within a couple of weeks of the interview.

chunks.heading: Running the team: solo, high-trust, little control
chunks.text:
- He chose to be a solo founder, partly because he knew he was hard to work with when younger. He pushes back on the "you need co-founders" narrative.
- He credits discipline and range: "I can code for an hour, do sales for two hours, and raise money for three hours", and says people are "so much more skilled than you think."
- He doesn't do outbound hiring. People find him through Buildspace, Twitter or email because he's public about the journey.
- His hiring filter is a short conversation: he asks who they are, not their skill set, and says he is a good judge of who he wants to be around.
- Example: Stefan taught him what design is on a whiteboard for about 10 minutes. What mattered to him was that Stefan treated him as an equal and could handle new information without ego.
- He keeps people through pivots by letting them shape the future. Roughly a year before, when unsure what came next, he had everyone stop for a week to build a pitch deck for the next thing. He then took all the ideas and made a path (Stefan's "telescope for finding the best people" idea fed into Nights & Weekends scaling).
- His management style: "I don't really have a vision." There's no task board. People tell him what they're working on in a sentence on Monday, and if it's bad, they tell each other. He creates open space and has little control but a lot of trust, while the final call is his.
- His schedule: about four hours of solo (IC) work in the morning, then afternoons helping teammates and running Nights & Weekends, parts of the campus, IRL, and a government function.
- Biggest mistake: pivoting Zip School from one-to-many live classes (thousands watching one teacher) to small live classes of about ten kids. He calls it a purely emotional decision. Furqan told him he was being emotional and he didn't see it. It wasted about six months.
- On the differentiator for success in Buildspace: people with no preconceived notion of right or wrong. The ones who quit say things like "I couldn't figure out marketing", and he asks whether marketing is even the problem. In his words, "the less you know the better in this industry."

chunks.heading: Identity, fame and perspective
chunks.text:
- He made YouTube videos from sixth grade (first shown only to family) and later posted them publicly so classmates would talk to him. "Farza" was an alter ego he made up. He was heavily bullied and says that is why he made the videos.
- His view on identity: "your identity is who you are, it's not what your work is." He says he's a son, brother and boyfriend and doesn't wrap his identity in Buildspace.
- On recognition: he's recognized a few times a week, treats it as proof the work means something, and takes it as motivation not to disappoint people. He never wanted to be famous.
- He distances himself from startup culture, which he finds cringe. He has very few founder friends, goes to no startup events and does almost no podcasts or talks.
- He mostly wants people to know "you're doing great", and says that expectations and narratives are stupid.
- He says he has no filter online, though he tries not to say "unhinged" things.
- His reason for doing this kind of work: to have fun and meet cool people, and he distrusts people who want more than that.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza's buildspace lecture on locking down an idea in week one. He argues ideas are starting points rather than good or bad, tells his Minecraft-tutoring-to-buildspace story, and gives a practical routine: write a plain one-liner, then post it publicly for feedback.

chunks.heading: Why Farza says ideas are overrated
chunks.text:
- He argues there is "no such thing as a good or bad idea" (his opinion, not fact). An idea is only "where you start your journey". You can't know where it ends up.
- Examples he cites: Angry Birds was Rovio's 51st game. Star Wars began as a 10-page story George Lucas wrote for friends and iterated on for years. The Dyson vacuum started as a drawing. Nike started as Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman wanting to make shoes for 50 people on a track team.
- "Great ideas are forged, they are not found." He compares it to taking a hammer to a rock until it starts to look like something good.
- Work is better with momentum than without: he would rather spend eight weeks working on any idea and learning than eight weeks looking for the perfect one.
- The idea should change in small ways every week, "kind of like a Pokemon".
- He says you never fully figure it out. Once an idea works, your goals, interests and the idea itself change (10 dollars becomes 100 dollars, 10 followers becomes 100). So don't feel everyone else has it figured out.
- Don't try to impress people with how important your idea is. You don't need to be "solving cancer".

chunks.heading: Farza's own path: Farza School to Zip School to buildspace
chunks.text:
- At 23 he spent about three months at his parents' house trying to find a "good idea". He wrote words from product websites on index cards, shuffled them and drew three at a time, 9am to 6pm daily. He says he could not stay on any idea longer than three days.
- He broke the loop by asking what he would work on if it were his last year on Earth. The answer was a school for kids teaching fun things like Minecraft servers, websites and Discord bots.
- In October 2019 he made "Farza School" cards and put them in mailboxes in rich parts of town. Nobody called. The only student was his cousin Samir, who said he'd rather do this every day than go to his actual school.
- That led him into homeschooling Facebook groups, where he ran polls. He then made a fake Facebook account saying "I have this app that helps people start a homeschool", and many parents said they'd want it. He built Zip Homeschool from a Webflow template.
- First paying customer: 90 dollars, from a parent named Lucy. The service grew from setup help to lesson plans and worksheets to him teaching kids on Zoom (for example about rockets), then hiring teachers.
- Zip School went somewhat viral among kids, then got funded by Y Combinator. He says the same core people and company became buildspace.
- His summary: "I literally could not have predicted any of this." He says he'd rather tell this story than Steve Jobs or Bill Gates stories, because he wants to show how real people make things happen.

chunks.heading: How to choose what to work on
chunks.text:
- Follow excitement and curiosity, however big or small. The number one reason people give up is that they stop being excited and things get hard.
- Don't pick something because it's trending or "sounds like a good idea". His example is B2B SaaS, which people pick for being good but then find boring. Do things because they're fun.
- Stuck? Pick something you're a big fan of and do something related. He loved League of Legends so he built an app around it. He loved Key & Peele so he made funny YouTube videos.
- If your idea already exists, that is validation: "you're not crazy". He cites Christopher Nolan making The Dark Knight after about 20 Batman movies. There is never a truly unique idea.
- Pick one idea and commit to it for the program rather than splitting across two or three. Let it evolve naturally, but don't bounce between unrelated things (movies, music, AI apps) every week.
- Do you have to solve a problem? He says not necessarily at the start. He says that to this day he doesn't know what problem buildspace solves, though he adds that to build a business you do need to solve a problem. His counterexamples: Justin Bieber and Mr Beast.
- Fear of getting copied: if someone copies you and wins, it "wasn't your destiny". Your idea works because you make it work, not because it is amazing.

chunks.heading: The one-liner test: make the idea clear, not good
chunks.text:
- Goal: a clear idea, not a "good" one. Be able to describe it in one sentence, ideally by the end of the session and at worst within a week.
- Vague: "an AI app", "a marketing agency", "a short film". Clearer: "an AI app that helps teachers make flashcards", "a marketing agency for seed-stage companies", "a short film about a robot that falls in love with a toaster".
- Once it's a sentence, the next step becomes obvious (for the toaster film: buy a toaster, record, write the script).
- Test: tell your mom, dad or a friend; they should instantly say "I get it". Don't over-complicate with problem/solution/market frameworks.
- Format: a one-liner (what it is) plus one or two sentences on how it works. Keep it under two lines, three at most. Expect it to improve over the six weeks. The buildspace one-liner itself changed for years.
- Examples he rated acceptable: "I'm writing a song a day until one goes viral" (Joe Yang); a personalized workout and meal plan generator; an AI-powered SQL editor with charts and dashboards; a YouTube channel explaining math and technology.
- Bad: buzzword copy like "an innovative AI-powered platform that revolutionizes how you discover people". He rates that a zero. Don't use buzzwords to impress.
- Live critiques: cut filler words like "platform" ("a mental health platform for teenagers" is unclear; "an iOS app where teenagers get daily breathing exercises" is clear). An app for ordering food before you get to the restaurant, with the food and table ready on arrival, was a 7 out of 10. "A short film about a bench in Central Park" was an 8 to 8.5.
- He deliberately avoids showing a "perfect 10" so as not to bias people. He says everyone already knows whether they understand an idea when it is told to them at a party.

chunks.heading: Getting the idea out and getting feedback
chunks.text:
- After writing the one-liner on a template (an "idea slide" with project name, one-liner and how it works), post it publicly the same day: Twitter, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok or a group chat. He says it is about having the courage to put it out there and using the internet to push the idea forward.
- Use a burner account if you're scared, but his view is "ship it to production". Keep the post simple: the slide, a line on why you're working on it, no hashtag spam.
- Give feedback to three other people's ideas in return. His line: to get feedback on your idea, start by giving feedback on others'. Last season this produced over 100,000 pieces of feedback.
- No excuses if nobody replies. He suggests showing a printed slide to 10 people in person and asking "do you get it?". Getting it out of your head makes you feel lighter and makes the idea public to friends.
- A short video where you explain your idea over a green-screen slide is a low-cost extra step. He argues "what do you have to lose": worst case you get better at talking about your work on camera, best case it pops.
- Weekly cadence: the number of participants drops each week (17,000 at kickoff, about 8,400 here). He treats that as a forcing function and says to network more seriously around week six with those who stay.

chunks.heading: Don't wait for permission
chunks.text:
- He highlights people who started immediately without being told: building a robot friend, a new guitar tool, taking online kinematics classes, editing videos, drawing schematics, making their first content.
- His message: "Don't sit here and wait for me to give you permission to start doing stuff." Do what feels right, but do something.
- Lock the idea in week one so you can commit for the remaining five weeks rather than wanting to switch in week four.
- The goal for the week: pick, clarify and finalize one idea. If you already have one, start building. Even people far along (revenue, subscribers) benefit, because a single idea needs hundreds of smaller ideas (video, product piece, marketing) and the same clarify-and-iterate process applies to each.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza reflects on a week where he proposed that AI companies pay for teaching people to build real things with their tools, and one agreed to $50k/month. He covers staying authentic when sponsored, thinking in steps rather than ceilings, productizing teaching into software, and using weekly deadlines.

chunks.heading: Proposing a business model: sell "teach people to build with your tool" to AI companies
chunks.text:
Farza spent the week working out how Make Something (his AI-education project) could become a business. He sent proposals to two companies:
- A big AI tooling company, which agreed to pay $50,000 a month after about one call. The final contract is still pending.
- One of the big AI labs, which he is still talking to about the same $50,000 a month.
- Pitch: "I will use your technology. I will show people your technology. I will teach them your tools." The aim is to get people building real things with those tools.
- If both close, Make Something would be at $100,000 a month, about $1M a year. He notes it had existed for under a month.

chunks.heading: Why AI companies will pay for it: tools are known, usage isn't
chunks.text:
- Farza argues the core problem AI companies face is that everyone knows the tools exist but few people build real things with them.
- His analogy is the computer. Most people were never taught to use one, but using it powerfully takes programming, marketing or design education.
- He argues the people building with AI are mostly those who were already building before. Few new people are coming in.
- IG ads and influencer marketing can't fix this. A million sign-ups on an AI builder product doesn't mean people will build real businesses or retain long term.
- His positioning is to help people build their own ideas and businesses with AI over the long term.

chunks.heading: Sponsorship and authenticity as the constraint
chunks.text:
- Farza hasn't said yes to the contract. He doesn't want to be a shill for these companies.
- He doesn't want to do a stream or piece of content "just cuz someone's paying me". He wants to talk about tools he actually uses in his workflows.
- He prides himself on authentic material. He would "rather just not do any of this at all" than plug a tool in front of his landing page because of payment.
- He contrasts himself with MrBeast plugging NordVPN. MrBeast can do that at a scale of billions. Farza's audience (people who make things, education) is at the scale of millions.

chunks.heading: Step-wise ceilings instead of big-market thinking
chunks.text:
- Farza doubts Make Something can make tens or hundreds of millions a year. He doesn't focus on that.
- He thinks in steps: can it make $10, $10,000, $100,000, a million? Each step is the next goal.
- He argues ideas rarely have a hard ceiling: "once you reach the ceiling there is always a way where you can break past that ceiling." Going from $1M to $5M a year would take more pushing and fresh ideas.
- He still treats Make Something as a side project and not yet a company. It might become one if the deals close.

chunks.heading: Productizing teaching: the AI screen-watching tutor
chunks.text:
- Farza and Julian, a co-founder trial partner, are exploring how to put the teaching experience into software.
- The product is an AI that watches your screen and guides you through building your first app with Codex. It sits as a Mac sidebar, talks to you and unsticks you.
- It doesn't write the code. It guides step by step: go to codex.com, download it, write your first prompt, get your app off localhost.
- The idea is that the best way to learn is a friend who is an expert sitting next to you.
- Launched at the previous Saturday stream, Mac only, to a subset of users. About 40 downloaded it and about 10 built their first app. It was buggy and is still very early.
- He wants to keep a human element in the content, but doesn't want to teach "how to build your first app with Codex" live every weekend.

chunks.heading: Live streams, content and growth numbers
chunks.text:
- Make Something runs one live stream every Saturday. Farza says the weekly deadline has been good for him: "I work really well with deadlines."
- Latest stream: about 1,000 signed up, about 400 showed up, about 200 built an app.
- Cumulative after about 3 weeks: more than 10,000 people reached, about 7,000 emails in the database, about 800 people shipped their first app, and a Discord of almost 1,000 people where they co-work daily.
- He hired a filmmaker friend in India to make Instagram videos. Farza says he loves writing content (scripts, hooks, the emotions) more than being on camera.
- He wanted more Saturday attendance and did only a little extra promotion.

chunks.heading: Paying users instead of influencers
chunks.text:
- He offered users who shipped their first app $40 to make a reel about the experience, instead of paying random influencers.
- Some made good reels, and he plans to keep experimenting.
- He doesn't "necessarily believe in UGC". The principle is to empower people who enjoy your thing to talk about it, and he dislikes giving it an official name.

chunks.heading: Raising money and the Buildspace déjà vu
chunks.text:
- Farza says he could raise roughly $500K to $4-5M now and keep control. He had a good, pressure-free experience with investors on his last company.
- He values that the market is open now, unlike 2021-2023, which he calls horrible.
- He doesn't want to raise "if I don't know what I'm working on".
- He feels like he is rebuilding Buildspace, a 5-year project. He likes that Make Something is a new brand with no baggage, so he can move fast and try things without pressure.
- He says there are no shortcuts: "how many cycles you put in" determines how much you learn and how fast you move. Experience doesn't let you recognize a great idea faster.
- He wants to work on what he loves and make it a good business, and says working with the right people matters as much as the project.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza live-teaches a college student to build a personal site, a paid journaling web app with accounts and Stripe, and an iPhone app using Lovable, Replit and Claude Code. The takeaways: AI agents collapse build cost, ideas can be small and already exist, and a few paying users is a real win.

chunks.heading: Farza's pitch: AI agents make building software a matter of knowledge, not coding skill
chunks.text:
- Farza argues the only thing separating people building cool things with AI from everyone else is "knowledge", not talent or creativity.
- He says a League of Legends music site that took him 6 months to code in 2016 (about 2 million users in two weeks) was rebuilt by AI in 6 minutes from one sentence.
- Coding agents differ from chat: you send one message and the agent works alone for 30-45 minutes, making its own decisions and needing no intervention.
- A build that once cost around $250,000 for a Noon-style app now costs "20 bucks at minimum, maybe like 100 bucks, 1,000 bucks at maximum".
- His proof: a Mac journaling app built in about 8 hours without knowing Swift, which got 2 million views and 10,000 downloads.
- His working method is to run two agents in parallel so he is never waiting on one.
- His 13-year-old self sold blank DVDs, and by 15 he made about $100,000 a year.

chunks.heading: Level 1: a personal landing page in Lovable instead of a resume
chunks.text:
- Farza starts beginners with a landing page, since it is only a website that shows information.
- Prompt: "make me a personal website", then paste in the person's whole LinkedIn and Twitter. The agent infers what to highlight, and it linked projects to their real URLs.
- The page was live on the internet in minutes. The follow-up edits took one prompt each: a light/dark mode toggle, a mobile layout, and a fix for a hallucinated LinkedIn link.
- He says a page like this beats a resume for job hunting: "If I got this website and I was hiring, I would jump on a call with you".
- Mobile layout is "notoriously difficult" for engineers, and it took one sentence.
- The agent picks the language (JavaScript) itself, and you can name one if you care.
- He tells people to give the agent the correct link when it hallucinates, and to re-prompt when something breaks.
- Lovable's free tier ran out mid-demo, and he calls it great for beginners with no idea what they are doing.

chunks.heading: Level 2: a full app with accounts, a database and payments in Replit
chunks.text:
- A full app differs from a landing page because it stores private user data, so it needs logins, a database, image storage and security.
- Replit created the database and picked the authentication service on its own from the request "visitors can make an account, all moments are private to the user".
- Prompting advice: "Describe what you want kind of like you'd be asking a real human being", as if briefing a software engineer.
- He sketched the UI in Excalidraw (a profile pic and date, a "new moment" button, a feed) and pasted it into the prompt as a PNG. Agents also accept a screenshot of a site to clone with changes.
- The example app, Moments, is a private visual journal: Instagram only for yourself.
- Replit built a landing page, signup, login and moment upload. It also added unrequested features such as a calendar and a "best moment" star.
- The agent can test its own app by driving a mini browser and recording video of the flow.
- He treats a human testing pass as non-negotiable. Bugs found live included a cropped image, a missing subscribe banner, a Stripe error and a build failure.
- Fix loop: tell the agent what is wrong, or click "debug with agent", and repeat until it works.

chunks.heading: Adding payments with Stripe and publishing
chunks.text:
- Prompt: add a $5/month subscription button after login. Replit proposed connecting Stripe and created the checkout page.
- Test with the fake card 4242 4242 4242 4242 while in sandbox mode, then connect a real Stripe account tied to a bank account and publish.
- Publishing was a single button that deployed to the internet with a URL. A custom domain such as moments.live is about $30 a year.
- Costs seen live: the Flappy Bird clone cost 58 cents and about 3 minutes, and the whole Moments app ran about $3 of credits by the time payments were added.
- Replit is about $20 a month, versus about $49 for Claude Code as he states it.
- The live Stripe checkout broke on stage with "internal server error" and was never fixed. He guesses it was a key or account mix-up and says some bugs cost "10, 20, 30 minutes".
- Pricing idea he floated: free for the first 10 entries then charge, or show only the 3 most recent entries free and charge for the rest. "Dumbest thing possible" was simple $5/month.

chunks.heading: Fast prototyping with games, and iterating by talking to the agent
chunks.text:
- He built a Flappy Bird clone with Batman as the bird in about 3 minutes for 58 cents, then iterated: "make it harder" (the agent raised gravity and pipe speed, shrank gaps and sped up spawning), then a daytime Superman skin.
- He notes the original Flappy Bird made $50,000 per day, and that anyone with a game idea can now build it in minutes.
- Agent edits are plain-language requests. The agent already holds the whole codebase and knows which file to change.
- He suggests being polite to the AI ("I say good morning to my AI every morning").
- The lightning button in Replit makes quick changes faster.

chunks.heading: Level 3: a native iPhone app with Claude Code and Xcode
chunks.text:
- Claude Code is "the hardest one to learn, but it's the best one" and runs in the terminal on your computer. Replit and Lovable run on the internet, while iPhone app code lives locally.
- Steps: create a new project in Xcode (free), open Claude Code in that folder, describe the app, answer its clarifying questions, approve its file permissions, then press play in Xcode to run a simulated iPhone.
- The demo prompt was a workout tracker for progressive overload that logs workouts and weights, with a welcome screen and onboarding questions (weight, height). Claude Code asked about workout type and detail level, then built it in minutes with working onboarding, exercise logging and saved history.
- iPhone apps are "notoriously difficult" with their own language (Swift). You can test on your own phone without App Store approval.
- He compares the idea to the workout app Strong, which he says makes millions of dollars a month.

chunks.heading: Idea selection and the $250 a month target
chunks.text:
- "You don't need a crazy innovative idea, you just need an idea that you enjoy that's useful to you."
- Don't make the next Uber or Airbnb, and don't worry that similar apps exist: "There's thousands of journaling apps" but yours is made for you and your friends.
- If 10 people pay $5 a month that is $50 a month and fine; software is built once and sold to everybody.
- Target he gives: $250 a month, meaning 25 people paying $10 a month. "If everyone here was making $250 a month, they'd be pretty happy."
- To start, find one person to pay, then five, then 10 to 25.
- His first-dollar story: at 13 he made $10 on eBay in about 5 minutes, compared with friends earning that in an hour at a grocery store.
- Perk from the event: a Replit partnership gave attendees one month free with the code "Farza", and Rork (a mobile app builder) offered one month free with "Farza Dubai".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza recounts a week where a shelved idea (Clicky) went viral while he felt lonely building solo. He explains why he ships stale ideas, values usage over views, calls top users to find direction, and assembles a small team rather than waiting for a co-founder.

chunks.heading: Founder loneliness and getting personal validation when building solo
chunks.text:
- Farza says being solo is "so difficult" emotionally. When Clicky went viral, he shipped late on a Monday night with no one to share it with.
- With a co-founder you high-five and get pizza. Solo, you "pat myself on the back, close my laptop, celebrate by drinking a glass of water," and go to bed.
- Solo, he says, "you have to really dig deep for personal validation." That is hard for anyone and harder when building.
- He says his worst emotional weeks come when the internet is most excited about what he's doing. Praise and inbound investor attention left him lethargic and flat, not happy.
- Loneliness is the emotion he is most prone to. His fix is to remember he is prone to it and recall that he has a partner, family and friends who support him.
- Not having a co-founder directly on the thing does not mean being alone.
- At 23 he was a "blind dog" sprinting forward and did not need anyone. At 30 he wants to collaborate.
- He credits his partner with keeping him sane and says he would never have returned to starting companies without her.

chunks.heading: Drive forward yourself and let people join
chunks.text:
- His belief: "the best way to find people and to work with people is by just driving forward yourself. And as you drive forward, hopefully other people hop in your car."
- He admits it is easier said than done. He lets himself be down for a day or three, then finds the will to keep going almost every time.
- He asked two friends he calls geniuses to start a company together. Both declined and stayed in their jobs, which saddened him.
- His read: it is not that something is wrong with him. Co-founder search takes time, and "timing is such a big thing."

chunks.heading: Forming a 30-day hack team in three days
chunks.text:
- After the users' feedback, he invited a few friends to SF for 30 days to hack on Clicky, new interfaces for agents, and education. They are not co-founders, just people working together in person.
- Four people agreed within about 3 days and bought tickets to arrive the following week:
  - A filmmaker flying from Bangalore to make videos.
  - An engineer he had worked with before, coming from Bali.
  - A neighbor who won a past Buildspace season.
  - A non-technical biomedical student from Houston who had just dropped out. He built the best custom Clicky implementation Farza saw, out of about 80 posted. His video had only about 80 views.
- Farza DM'd the Houston student, FaceTimed him, and the next day he agreed to fly out. Farza is paying for the flight.
- Clicky was open-sourced, which is how people made custom versions. Farza plans to keep the current version open source and make future code closed source.

chunks.heading: Take shelved ideas off the shelf and ship them
chunks.text:
- Farza says he hates an idea sitting stale: "every idea should be just taken off the shelf and just thrown out into the world. And you just see what happens."
- Clicky had reached about 10 users the week before. He judged it a "shitty idea" and was letting it die.
- On Monday night he recorded a demo in about 10 minutes at the YC office, posted it on Twitter, closed his laptop and went to dinner. By the time he got back it was going viral, reaching roughly 1 to 2 million views over 2 to 3 days.
- Views mean little to him: "virality means absolutely nothing to me." He says a video of a celebrity dancing with AI would get a million views and a video of himself dancing maybe a thousand. Usage is what matters.
- That night he found the Mac app had API keys hard-coded, so anyone could steal them. He spent about 2 hours rebuilding it with a back end and launched around 10:30pm.
- By the next morning there were thousands of downloads.

chunks.heading: Talking to your top users instead of guessing
chunks.text:
- When he doubted whether to continue, he did "the most simple thing possible": he looked at PostHog analytics, picked 10 of the top 25 users by usage, and emailed them to book calls the next day. He spoke with about four or five on Friday.
- Numbers about 4 days after launch: about 25,000 messages sent, about 4,000 unique downloads, and almost 600 users retained at day 4 (using it every day).
- Use cases he heard:
  - A founder writing all his LinkedIn content with it.
  - A video editor moving from After Effects to DaVinci.
  - A pro Xcode developer getting feedback on his iPhone app's animations.
  - A guy watching anime with it and discussing characters and story.
- His takeaway: "As a founder, you have no freaking idea who's going to use your product and why they're going to use it until you put it out there." He had launched Clicky as an AI teacher, and users found their own uses.
- Those uses excited him more than the teaching angle did. He wasn't excited about teaching as a business or long-term product.
- Every call ended the same way. They asked what was next, he said he probably wouldn't keep working on it, and each user urged him to continue. He notes that usually the founder is the one pitching users, and here it was reversed.

chunks.heading: How Farza treats user feedback
chunks.text:
- The founder's job is "not to come up with the product out of my brain." It is to see how people use the product, what they find useful, and guide it.
- He disagrees with "build what people tell me to." If a user says "build this," he won't build exactly that.
- He treats feedback as inspiration: he listens, processes it, and builds it into the product in some way, not one-to-one. He jokes it is like being an LLM with users prompting him: tokens in, his own output out.

chunks.heading: Using a group office hours one-liner to find an idea
chunks.text:
- At YC group office hours on Monday, founders explain what they're working on to about 25 people. Farza calls this "very underrated" and used to make Buildspace students do it.
- He found it hard to explain a project when he did not know what he was working on, but said it is a good exercise because it forces a one-liner.
- His one-liner that day: "a Pinterest but for companies," where a team collects things that inspire them as they browse (tweets, research papers, articles) into one shared knowledge base. He liked it more after saying it aloud and built a simple version that day.
- He showed it to his YC partner Aaron, who gave him more ideas and a comparison to workflows at another big-company CEO.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza argues the biggest AI + education opportunity is end-to-end "machines" that take someone from a 2/10 to a 6/10 in their ability to pursue a goal, not tools that help students study. Pure learning is hard to monetize, while outcomes are what people pay for. AI could finally scale the accountability, structure and motivation that only high-touch human programs delivered.

chunks.heading: Education as human-capital machines, not study tools
chunks.text:
- Farza thinks AI + education is stuck on "helps students pass exams" products: upload a PDF for flashcards, upload a lecture for notes, AI teacher lesson builders, language apps, AI tutors over video courses. He calls these "nothing that fresh" compared with how AI is reshaping robotics, self-driving cars, drones, coding and even memes.
- His core claim: "Learning, education, upskilling, studying" describe the act, not the outcome. Very few people learn just to learn; they learn to do something (close a first deal, start a YouTube channel, go freelance and quit a job).
- Examples of act-over-outcome products he lists: language apps with a 500-day streak where you still can't speak Spanish; platforms with thousands of hours of content nobody watches; certifications that look good on LinkedIn but don't change capability; AI tools that summarize lectures and generate quizzes for an exam you forget in a week. He says none of this is bad, but it is optimized for learning rather than doing.

chunks.heading: Why "learning" alone is a weak business
chunks.text:
- "You can only monetize straight up 'learning' so much." People won't pay much or for long for learning without a clear result in sight.
- This makes the market look like an ocean of students with terrible retention, jobless people without money to spend, or consumers who pay for a few years as "lifelong learners".
- His chain of consequences: education companies look "small", so investors don't invest, so founders don't start them, so founders move to more lucrative things like "verticalized B2B voice agents for customer service".
- He says course businesses such as Coursera, Udacity, Duolingo, Skillshare and Masterclass can be good businesses but are weak "machines" (a typical buyer buys a course or two, never finishes, and moves from maybe 2/10 to 3/10).

chunks.heading: Reframe: build "human capital factories"
chunks.text:
- Farza argues these aren't really education companies; they are "companies that build new human capital". A company that does its job produces inventors, designers, musicians, engineers, doctors and founders, the people who change reality.
- His mental model is the "machine": input a person at X/10 in their ability to impact the world and pursue their goals in some domain, output them at a higher number.
  - Stanford: an 18-year-old who is a 3/10 goes in; a 6/10 on average comes out after four years.
  - YC: founders enter around 5-6/10 and leave around 8/10, because money, mentorship and customers accelerate them.
  - The Knowledge Society (TKS), an after-school accelerator for 13-17 year-olds, where a kid at 1/10 in self-belief, ambition and ability to tackle hard problems can leave at 5/10 or better through projects, tight mentorship, internships, research and startups.
  - buildspace: designed so someone enters a 2/10 and exits a 6/10 on average in their ability to start a business, reach financial goals and work on their own ideas. He notes it ended up quite valuable and, 1.5 years after the company closed, he still gets near-daily messages about past participants raising rounds, landing dream jobs or starting side hustles.
- He cautions you can't guarantee outcomes ("do this and you'll make $100,000"), but you can improve someone's chances of reaching them.

chunks.heading: What actually transforms people (and the scaling problem)
chunks.text:
- "It sure as hell isn't content." Content is as free and diverse as ever and we're not all geniuses. Transformation comes from "the right balance of learning, accountability, and structure. All while properly maintaining your motivation." The best human mentors do this naturally.
- Machines with strong guaranteed outcomes are high-touch and hard to scale: YC takes roughly 1,000 companies a year, MIT roughly 2,000 undergraduates, TKS supports about 1,000 kids a year. Top bootcamps that guarantee jobs and elite apprenticeships are tough to access because humans must lead them, so a tiny percent of humanity gets the best machines.
- He argues these succeed arguably because they don't scale, and says he is not telling people to only build things that scale ("I rather live in a world with MIT vs without").
- buildspace took the opposite approach, scaling to 100,000+ people per year as "low touch, but high access", designed as an open game anyone could join.
- He rejects the lazy version of the idea: "Okay lets build AI Steve Jobs and we can scale mentorship to 100M people" ("If that was the solution, it'd be done already").

chunks.heading: The AI opportunity: end-to-end machines per goal
chunks.text:
- His thesis: the biggest AI + education opportunity is not helping people study random skills, but building end-to-end machines that output human capital, taking someone anywhere at 2/10 to 6/10 in pursuing a specific goal.
- Imagine a separate machine for each goal: becoming a YouTuber, an author, a coder who gets a job, a salesperson, a filmmaker.
- He expects "education companies that democratize the ability for people to actually become something." Tools alone won't create mass change.
- The models "haven't been pushed to push humans yet", which he calls very under-explored but worthwhile. It is "not exactly a 'learning' problem": it is human psychology and retaining motivation and drive.

chunks.heading: Pakistan case study: a human acting like an AI
chunks.text:
- A year before writing, in Pakistan, Farza helped a 21-year-old learn to build a Shopify store, source clothes locally and sell them on Facebook Marketplace.
- His involvement: two check-in meetings a week, mostly setting weekly goals and reframing "I can't do this" thoughts.
- Result: the kid reached $250 a month, which is what his father earned per month as a driver. In Farza's view he went from 1/10 to 5/10, learning basic web design, marketing and customer service, and built a basic business.
- Farza says he "may as well have been an AI model he was talking to". The questions he poses for an AI version:
  - Could a "magical AI cursor" have taught him Shopify?
  - Could the AI hold a weekly call to get him to his first $10?
  - Could it tell him where he was messing up?
  - Could it keep his mental state in check?
  - Could it connect him with similar people locally?
- He thinks all of this is within what models can do and can be generalized, to a would-be designer in Morocco, an author in Berlin, or a genetics student in India aiming to solve epilepsy.

chunks.heading: Call to action
chunks.text:
- Farza says such companies "won't be 'education companies.' They'll be human capital factories," and could be among the most valuable ever built, since startups, cures, movies and inventions all come from people.
- He is looking for a co-founder (early, still unsure exactly what he'll build) and asks interested people to email a few lines about themselves and what they want to work on.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza argues founders shouldn't choose between speed-running to $1M ARR on a thin AI wrapper and building a long-term dream; he wants both. Using his 2010 dropshipping days and the Nike story, he shows how a money-printing engine can fund a generational product, and urges founders to learn from winners instead of doubting themselves.

chunks.heading: Speed-running money vs. building the dream: Farza's "both" position
chunks.text:
- Farza says founder friends are debating whether to build "something generational" or just make money by "speed running to $1M ARR on some iOS AI app."
- He sees founders who have grinded for years on massive problems questioning their core philosophies. The choice they frame: "Do we build a money printer or do we continue to focus on building the dream."
- Part of the pull comes from seeing people on YouTube and Twitter hit $1M or $5M in under a year, which makes founders ask "Am I doing something wrong??"
- Another subset dismisses those apps as "just a wrapper grown by mindless UGC on Instagram," useless or a distraction. Farza pushes back on that dismissal.
- His conclusion: "Money, or dreams? Both. It must be both."

chunks.heading: The 2025 AI app playbook mirrors 2010 dropshipping
chunks.text:
- Farza dropshipped in 2010, arbitraging random niches: wrap a product in cleaner messaging, run ads, profit.
- He says 99% of the AI apps launching in 2025 follow the same playbook: find a niche, wrap the latest model (built via Cursor) with cleaner messaging, and pay TikTok college kids instead of buying ads.
- The loop of find niche, build software, distribute gets easier every month, so more people do it.
- The result: in 2025 he sees the same thing as in 2010 at age 14, people aged 14-21 "just printing on the internet." He calls it "pretty awesome."
- He does not treat the playbook as trivial. Anyone can wrap a model, just as anyone could dropship, but hitting $100K a month on anything is "difficult as fuck." The winners are "truly obsessed," with relentless execution and genuine love for the game.

chunks.heading: Why most wrapper businesses die
chunks.text:
- Farza's own dropshipping business is gone, along with most of the early-2010s dropshipping businesses.
- His team was full-time arbitraging a short-term opportunity until little was left to arbitrage. Facebook ad acquisition costs rose, CAC became "ridiculous," consumers realized everyone was wrapping Alibaba, and sales dipped.
- Almost nobody was building a true product that became core to people's lives. The dropshipping businesses that survived put effort into their own formula, product or secret sauce.
- He expects something similar to happen to many of today's explosive AI apps.

chunks.heading: Farza's own stance: find the large opportunity, but learn from the money printers
chunks.text:
- For himself, he wants to find the large opportunity and have the patience to build the dream. He does not want to lower his long-term ambition just to hit a short-term money number.
- He is also "inspired as fuck" by 16-year-olds hitting $1M ARR on iOS apps they make in 30 days, and says he needs to learn everything he can from them.
- His view: "a great short-term money printer has a high chance of turning into a generational product with the right vision. I'd rather have an engine, than not."

chunks.heading: The Nike example: a money printer can fund the vision
chunks.text:
- Nike spent its first 10 years as a "wrapper" around Onitsuka Tigers from Japan, dropshipping their shoes.
- Phil Knight kept growing the business, built a money printer, and kept growing the vision.
- One day Nike started making its own shoes. "50 years later we all wear Nikes."
- Farza uses this as proof that wrapping and reselling early can be the engine that eventually funds a real product.

chunks.heading: Ego and ambition as failure modes
chunks.text:
- "Ambition can be a poison."
- Ego can stop founders from doing things that work in the short term because they believe their way of building products is "better," less cringe, or better for humanity.
- His position: "There is no right/wrong."
- If you are purely obsessed with speed-running money, that is great, but he suggests putting some "braincells" into the long term.
- If you are purely obsessed with being the next Apple and building a company that lasts decades but you are at $0 or close to it, that is great, but "perhaps go and make some money."

chunks.heading: Advice for founders grinding for years without a breakout
chunks.text:
- "Keep your eyes and ears open 24/7. Constantly learn how this game is changing."
- When you see someone winning online, don't think "Damn what am I doing wrong." Think "What can I learn from this person and their work."
- "Just adjust your game plan vs crumbling."
- He would hate a world where people dream smaller or lower their ambitions just for a monetary goal, and equally hate one where people ignore reality and stay stuck in their dreams forever.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza, founder of buildspace, explains why he stopped faking a grand "vision" in 2019 and admitted he didn't know where he was going. Honesty attracted teammates and investors who trusted a track record of doing what he said. A long-term vision is a skill built from years of immersion in one craft, not a flash of genius.

chunks.heading: Starting a company without a vision: trust and consistency over theatre
chunks.text:
Farza raised $12M for his company (buildspace) and hired a strong team while openly saying "I have no idea" when asked for his 10-year plan. He argues a founder does not need a vision to start.

- For years he performed as a "visionary" because books and role models (great CEOs, directors, writers) suggested a god-given vision was required.
- He says that act was painful and "That wasn't me." He is not a natural storyteller or persuasive speaker; he is a "quiet grinder" who finds answers by working toward them.
- His rule: "don't be someone you're not." Improve yourself and fix your flaws, but never pretend to be someone else.

chunks.heading: What changed in 2019: admitting he had no vision
chunks.text:
In 2019, at 23, Farza stopped faking confidence and started telling the truth: he did not know exactly where he was going, only that he was going toward "something".

- He could not describe the next 365 days, let alone 10 years.
