- His standard line to hires and investors: "Down to figure it out together?"
- Many high-value hires and investors looked at him like a fool and never came back. Many people thought he was an idiot.
- The cost was real, but he accepted it.

chunks.heading: Honesty as a filter for hires and investors
chunks.text:
Being upfront about not having a vision changed who joined and who invested.

- It attracted people willing to "navigate the unknown", who did not need a weekly vision or pep talk from him and who trusted the team would work it out together.
- These people make up the buildspace team today.
- Investors worked the same way: they knew he had no polished vision of the future but trusted him to figure out the long-term magic.

chunks.heading: Why people trusted him: results, not persuasion
chunks.text:
Farza says trust came from a track record, not from being a persuasive visionary.

- Most people say they will do something and then you never hear from them for two years.
- His pattern: say he will do something, do it, then update people on the results, whether he failed or succeeded.
- He held this pattern for many years.
- His summary: "Just doing the work vs playing theatrics." Trust was "built on results".

chunks.heading: How a long-term vision actually forms
chunks.text:
He is clear that a long-term view is eventually necessary: fantastic things are not built on 1-2 year timelines and often take 10-20 years. But the vision is a skill built over time, not a flash of genius.

- You cannot force a vision. It comes "bit by bit, over years and years" from dedicating yourself to a single craft.
- His movie example: Year 1 make a movie, Year 2 make another. By Year 3 you have learned enough to have a better vision for Year 3. Years 3-4 you make two more and learn what scripts to write, how to advertise, who to hire for the set. Year 5's vision gets clearer.
- By Year 10 you have a better 10-20 year vision and are "100X more equipped" to execute it.
- Swap movies for a generational company, the world's best sushi, or anything else.

chunks.heading: The fog of war and trusting the daily work
chunks.text:
Farza describes the required mindset as boring: trust that doing the daily work to the best of your ability, while dedicated to the craft, will make things figure themselves out.

- Trust in yourself is "everything".
- Many give up because "the fog of war" is intense. He says he has thought about giving up hundreds of times.
- His own timeline: only now, nearly 5 years, thousands of work days, millions in revenue and a full team later, is he starting to have a long-term vision for the work and the company's future. He stresses "5. Damn. Years. Later."
- He now feels clear and excited about the long-term work, with good people alongside him.

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text:
- You do not need a vision to start; a vision is something you work toward.
- Trust that doing the work gets you there.
- Do not play a role. Be yourself, admit what you do not know, and let honesty filter in people who want to figure it out with you.
- Build credibility by repeatedly saying what you will do, doing it, and reporting results.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains how a16z invested $2M in ZipHomeschool without a formal pitch or competitive process. He built in public, ran weekly progress calls with the investors, pivoted to a viral product, and let momentum do the selling. a16z later doubled down on buildspace.

chunks.heading: How Farza approached raising from a16z as a solo, first-time founder
chunks.text:
- Farza was a solo founder who had never raised money. He had built things since age 13, including products with 1M+ users, but never a startup.
- In 2019 he saw pitching as "cringe" and didn't want to learn it.
- His philosophy: build something really cool, talk about it online, and people will reach out and invest.
- He was building ZipHomeschool alone at his Mom's house. It was software that helps parents create a legal homeschool for their child, which he compared to "Stripe Atlas, but for homeschools."
- He shipped the MVP and got his first customer in the first week.
- Four months in he had about 50 customers and solid momentum.
- The more he talked about progress online, the more good people reached out to help.

chunks.heading: How the a16z conversation started and went
chunks.text:
- In May 2020 a16z sent him a cold email, and the first call went well.
- On the call he talked about customers, growth, and his vision for an operating system for the next 10M homeschoolers. He did not run a polished pitch.
- When a16z asked how much he was raising, he was honest and told them he was a noob. He says he is "honest to a fault" and says exactly what he is thinking.
- Being upfront did not turn them off. Anne Lee Skates and Connie Chan agreed to a next step.

chunks.heading: Weekly updates instead of a competitive process
chunks.text:
- For the next two months he spoke with a16z once a week for 30 minutes. Each call was a progress update plus brainstorming new ideas.
- Many people told him not to do this and to run a "competitive" fundraising process. He thought that was a dumb game and didn't do it.
- Why the cadence worked for both sides:
  - a16z got more data on him every week.
  - He kept building. If the company blew up, they would probably invest. If not, he would "just end up profitable."

chunks.heading: Letting traction drive the outcome
chunks.text:
- During those two months he made a big pivot from legal software to "Twitch for teachers," where teachers streamed live classes to thousands of kids.
- It went viral, with 100,000 class joins a week and millions of minutes streamed a week. The company was still just him.
- After the two months a16z invested $2M. He says he got the valuation he wanted.
- Papers were signed and money wired about a month after the call that confirmed the investment.

chunks.heading: His takeaway on fundraising
chunks.text:
- He sees many people waste time "playing the game of finding investors," or use it as an excuse for lack of progress.
- His position: "you simply need to put out really good work to an audience that grows over a long horizon. That is it."
- Public progress attracts inbound interest, so he built in public instead of chasing investors.
- Leaning on a friend (Furqan) through a hard period, with a weekly talk about the company's problems, gave him strength.

chunks.heading: The follow-on raise
chunks.text:
- About two years later, with the same team, company and cap table, he pivoted away from K-5 to a new idea that became buildspace.
- buildspace grew big and raised $10M, with half coming from a16z, who doubled down.
- His closing advice: "Keep your head up. Stay shipping."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza adds a third reason companies die beyond failing to raise or co-founder conflict: the founder slides into a negative mental spiral and can't solve daily problems. He explains how exhaustion compounds into irritability and self-blame, and shares his personal system for catching a spiral within 7-14 days and resetting.

chunks.heading: Spiraling is a third reason startups die, alongside failed fundraising and co-founder conflict
chunks.text:
Farza argues that most early-stage companies he has seen die did not fail from failed fundraising or co-founder conflict. They died because the founder ended up in a downward mental spiral and could not catch themselves. He says this applies to anyone who creates something from nothing, including creators, musicians and researchers, and that nobody warned him about it.

- Common advice he was given: companies die because 1) the founder couldn't raise or 2) co-founders had internal problems.
- His addition: "The founder simply ends up in a downward spiral, and can't catch themselves."
- He thinks it goes unmentioned because it is "just isn't as cool to talk about" as other startup topics.

chunks.heading: How the founder spiral unfolds
chunks.text:
The spiral starts with physical depletion, which makes everyday startup problems unsolvable, which deepens the negative state.

- **Trigger example:** 4-6 days in a row of 5-6 hours of sleep a night, not eating proper meals, and long working stretches with little movement. This leaves most people very tired.
- **New problems arrive anyway:** a growth experiment fails, cash runs low, the product turns out not to be great.
- **The tired founder can't cope:** no patience or mental strength to solve them. Annoyance at teammates and loved ones grows, the fuse gets shorter, annoyance turns into sadness, then self-blame ("not good enough").
- **It compounds:** the founder returns the next day and faces a new set of problems they can't solve, "because you can't even seem to solve the ones inside your own head."
- **Typical ending:** after roughly 3-6 months of spiraling the founder quits and the company or initiative dies.

chunks.heading: Catching a spiral early: Farza's warning signs and check-ins
chunks.text:
Farza says he has no general solution and is "not a psychologist or therapist", only what works for him. His approach is to catch the spiral in the first 7-14 days.

- **Signals he watches for:** 1) getting annoyed at others much faster than usual, 2) really low energy.
- **Daily journaling** is part of how he notices.
- **Self check-in:** a couple of times a month he asks himself "am I spiraling?"
- **Why speed matters:** "The longer it takes me to recognize the spiral, the worse it gets, and the harder it is for me to muster the energy to get out of it."

chunks.heading: Farza's reset protocol when he realizes he's spiraling
chunks.text:
When he realizes he is spiraling, he does the following:

1. Stop everything.
2. Admit to himself that he has lost to his emotions and is spiraling, and that this is okay.
3. Go home.
4. Spend one day doing things that give him energy. For him that means watching movies in theatres, running, sitting in a sauna or cold plunge (most effective for him), or an hour in a sensory deprivation tank.

After that day he returns to a solid routine of eating, sleeping and exercising.

chunks.heading: His own history of spirals
chunks.text:
- **Worst spiral:** nearly 2 years, from ages 18 to 20. He says he can't believe he made it out. What got him out was discovering "a deep love for programing", which gave him enough energy to leave a very dark place.
- **Last bad spiral (more than 45 days):** over 5 years before the essay (written Aug 2023). He spent 2 straight weeks doing nothing but exercising really hard, eating right and watching movies.
- **Since then:** "nearly spiral-free". He still spirals occasionally but almost always catches it within the first 2 weeks.

chunks.heading: Why founders are especially exposed, and what to do
chunks.text:
- Farza says founders are "**very susceptible** to spiraling and getting very sick from it" because their days are long, hard and full of problems from outside pressure.
- His prescription: "build that internal system that protects you." Don't let emotions rule you.
- If you are spiraling now, he advises taking a step back today or tomorrow and being easy on yourself. He compares a spiraling founder to "a car that's overheating": slow down first, then do things that energize you or bring joy, then make space to plan how to slow the spiral further.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza recruits four people (software, film, design, content) for a 3-month paid sprint in SF with no fixed idea. He lays out how he approaches the earliest, unknown stage of a company: a tiny team, daily shipping, ruthless ideas, and a hard deadline.

chunks.heading: Hiring a small "dream team" to explore before committing to an idea
chunks.text:
Farza is assembling a 4-person team in San Francisco for a 3-month stint (rough dates: May 14 to Aug 14) to find a new company together. He is explicit that he doesn't yet know what the company is.

- Possible directions he floats: "maybe its an ai consumer app," "maybe it's a vr game," "maybe its a new lightbulb company."
- He says he is not at the stage where he can offer "some big beautiful vision" to get people hyped. For that, he points people to OpenAI or SpaceX.
- He describes the stage as "that early unknown stage no one really talks about," where you throw things out and see what resonates.
- He admits this phase "is not very sexy" and "can be exhausting."

chunks.heading: Why he's doing the early phase with a team instead of alone
chunks.text:
- For his previous companies, he usually navigated the earliest, unclear stage alone, and only brought people on "once i feel like i have something that can float."
- This time he wants to do it differently, with others from day one.
- He believes in "the power of a small group of like-minded people essentially tinkering daily." In his view, this is "where every big vision or big company starts."
- The daily loop: get inspired, make something, share it, and try to find something completely new together.
- He considers this more exciting than starting from a fixed vision.

chunks.heading: The offer and terms
chunks.text:
- 4 people, 3 months.
- Farza flies each person out and gets them a place in SF.
- $10k per month base pay.
- The team works together every day at the 42,000 sqft Founders Inc campus in Fort Mason, SF, which he calls home to "the best builders in the world."
- Applications are expected to number a few hundred; he says he can't reply to everyone, but those who look like a fit hear from him by May 1.
- Applications go through a Tally form.

chunks.heading: The four roles and why that mix
chunks.text:
He wants one person for each of these:

- **Software person:** "an obsessed developer."
- **Film maker:** someone who wants to make movies.
- **Designer:** "you know how to make people feel."
- **Content creator:** "you know how to go viral."

His stated belief is that this group "can build nearly anything, and take over the world together." The mix covers building, making it feel good, telling the story, and distributing it.

chunks.heading: Success and failure conditions are set up front
chunks.text:
- If in 3 months the team "makes magic" and reaches millions of users and hundreds of thousands in revenue, they keep going.
- If they get nothing, "the team will self-destruct. like team rocket from pokemon."
- Even in the failure case, he frames it as 3 months spent in "the most beautiful city in the world" trying their hardest.
- This is a time-boxed bet with a clear kill criterion, so nobody is stuck in a vague, open-ended project.

chunks.heading: Operating principles for the exploration phase
chunks.text:
- "We'll be ruthless with ideas."
- "We will try a lot of things."
- "We will ship a lot."
- The goal is "to learn fast. and grow. not to look cool."
- Farza has been making things for 15 years and says this is a new company start, not a continuation of past ones.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza and Julian sold a simple 3-day live Zoom program (idea, small version, first dollar) via one LinkedIn post, making $1,400 in hours. The AI chatbot was hidden inside the program and used to surface mental blockers. The core lesson: people are held back by psychology, not knowledge, and the AI piece works best when packaged around a goal and done live with others.

chunks.heading: Selling a 3-day "first dollar" program instead of an AI chatbot app
chunks.text:
- Farza and Julian time-boxed the project to 5 days. They first assumed a mobile app, then dropped it: a standalone AI chatbot ("use my AI chat bot to help you work through your mental barriers") was something they felt they would never use themselves. Farza says he only puts out things he himself would convert on or use.
- Instead they sold a simple, easy-to-understand 3-day program, announced in a LinkedIn post on Sunday night. They made the product on Monday and ran the first session on Tuesday.
- Within a few hours the post brought in over $1,400 and the first group. They charged money partly because Julian wanted Fred Again tickets in NYC.
- The final group was 35 people, including a teacher making worksheets for other teachers, a 65-year-old journalist working on AI for reporters, and a photographer who wanted to help others become photographers. Most had no clear idea at the start.
- They deliberately left AI out of the pitch: "No one wakes up and wants to use AI for mental breakthroughs. So, why sell it when people don't even know they want it? I rather package it differently."
- Takeaway: "No one signs up for 'builder therapy.' But tell them the goal is their first dollar in 3 days and they'll work through whatever's in the way."

chunks.heading: Program structure: lecture plus a shared product session
chunks.text:
- Three sessions of 1.5 hours each, all on Zoom, with about 70% lecture from Farza and Julian and about 30% solo work in the product.
- Daily goals:
  - Day 1: come up with an idea.
  - Day 2: make a small version and show someone.
  - Day 3: make your first $.
- After lecturing, they put on music and had everyone use the product together. Making the AI part a group activity made it feel more magical, and let them prime people on how to have an effective conversation with the bot.
- His principle: "With bots, the quality of the conversation is the product. So anything that can make that feel better will make everything feel better."
- He notes none of the 35 participants got a 1-on-1 call.

chunks.heading: The product: free-write, then a bot that digs deeper
chunks.text:
- Julian built it in a few hours. Flow:
  1. Click the day you're on.
  2. Write freely for 15 minutes on that day's topic.
  3. Have a 15-minute conversation with a chatbot using a special prompt that takes the entry and digs deeper, on the idea or on the person's mindset.
- Participants were told the founders would read all messages and notes, but to write openly anyway.
- On Day 1 people wrote and chatted deeply. Farza says the entries went far beyond "I wanna make a project," touching fear of judgement and family relationships (one person described an elder brother blocking them from building).
- This confirmed his view that participants didn't need more motivation, knowledge or "another startup school." They needed to work through their mental blockers.
- Afterward he had Claude Code read everyone's bot chats, pull out the "breakthrough moments" and quote users directly.

chunks.heading: Why people don't start: psychology, not money or knowledge
chunks.text:
- Farza's thesis: the main barrier isn't money, knowledge or motivation. People don't understand their own psychology and carry hundreds of mental blockers about why they "can't" or aren't "ready."
- Example: a friend of his cousin wanted to become a content creator. He pointed out she already had an IG account and a phone camera, and suggested filming a 15-second Reel on the spot. She got nervous and refused out of fear of judgement. His point: giving her more knowledge wouldn't fix that.
- He estimates this is where about 90% of people are: they have the ability but "shoot themselves in the foot before they even begin."
- Common blockers he lists:
  - "I'm not smart enough to do this idea yet."
  - "If I make something, and it isn't perfect, and it fails, what then."
  - "All my ideas are small and useless compared to everyone else."
  - "It's not the right time, I'm busy with school."
  - "This idea will never make money."
- His framing of the opportunity: unlock more people to believe in themselves, teach them the skills, and have them go for it. He says productizing that would be one of the most important initiatives.
- His own method in 1-on-1 chats: question the core belief instead of arguing with it, e.g. "Why do you believe something must be good to post it? How can you know what good or bad is if you've never even posted anything? Who are you trying to impress?"

chunks.heading: Charging money was the deepest blocker
chunks.text:
- Day 3 (make money day) surfaced the deepest limiting beliefs. Many participants wouldn't charge because they felt what they had wasn't good enough.
- Farza treats this as diagnostic: Why does something have to be "good" to charge? Are you more afraid of people saying no, or of being rejected outright? Why do you care so much?
- The 30 minutes of AI-assisted introspection led many participants to breakthroughs or reframed beliefs, and some went from "idk what I'm doing" to first paying customers in 3 days.

chunks.heading: Using models to push humans, and the buildspace lesson
chunks.text:
- Farza and Julian both use Claude Opus to talk through their own mental barriers, and see it as a strong outside observer of one's actions and beliefs. Farza has long thought models should be used "to push humans."
- Buildspace context: Nights & Weekends season 5 had over 120,000 people. He wished he could have given every participant a 1.5-hour 1-on-1, but human mentors don't scale (tiny supply, huge demand). He believes thousands were lost to the stories they told themselves.
- In 2024 buildspace had no way to help people with this because the models weren't good enough. Now they are.
- Earlier history he cites: TeamMood at 19 (37 participants, 5 mentors, each person assigned a public repo so progress was visible; 10 people started their first projects after 8 weeks), then zipschool and buildspace.

chunks.heading: Takeaways Farza draws
chunks.text:
- Live format matters: the product alone as a standalone app likely wouldn't have been as effective. "Live remains extremely under explored in tech."
- People won't opt into AI introspection, but in a room with others, with a prompt and music, "suddenly they're writing things they've never said out loud."
- "30 minutes of the right questions > 30 hours of tutorials."
- He frames his work as "building stages where people give themselves permission to try." It was a roughly 4-day project and he is unsure where it goes next, but plans to carry the learnings forward.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A personal essay where Farza explains why he is joining YC a second time at 30 without a fixed idea. He contrasts the naivety of founding at 23 with the clarity of 30, and why he chooses to build over taking a safer job or VC path. Mindset-focused, with little tactical growth content.

chunks.heading: Farza rejoins Y Combinator at 30 with no fixed idea
chunks.text:
- In April 2026, Farza joined Y Combinator for a second time. His first batch was in 2020, when he was 23. The second batch started the week he wrote the post.
- He says he doesn't yet have a clear direction: "Not fully sure what I'm working on yet."
- He is a little scared to start a company again but mostly excited. After his last company, he "never thought I'd start anything again in my life" because it was so tough.
- He says he'll "never be 'ready'", so he's going for it.

chunks.heading: Starting a company at 23 versus 30
chunks.text:
- At 23 (YC in 2020), he had naivety. At 30 he knows how difficult building a company is.
- He describes himself as having "the naivety of a 19 year-old, but, with the mental of a guy who's been through a lot and learned a lot."
- He notes most people in YC are aged 19-24, and he is bullish on his mix of naivety and experience.
- He credits the last two years, which he calls "very healing", and a lot of work on himself for making a second attempt possible.

chunks.heading: Why he chose building over the safe path
chunks.text:
- He acknowledges the safer path: most founders end up as VCs or in high-tier jobs at big companies. He says he doesn't blame them, and that this path would be easier and more secure, especially as he starts thinking about family.
- He has been offered many great jobs. Each time he considers one, a voice in his head says to give his visions a shot.
- He has no specific "this is the idea I'm excited about". It's more a feeling of "I should explore my ideas... I would regret it if I didn't."
- He thinks the timing is unusually good: "Especially in 2026, at the epicenter of one of the greatest inventions of my lifetime." He also says "There's never been a better time to work on the ideas in my head."
- His stance is to accept the risk: "Maybe I flop, maybe I don't, only one way to find out." He closes with "We must be brave!"

chunks.heading: Operating approach during the batch
chunks.text:
- He plans to spend little time documenting and to focus mostly on building.
- He expects to launch a lot of random stuff over the following weeks.
- He will post one weekly update on YouTube, which has been more fun for him lately than writing on Substack. The first video covers how the YC opportunity happened, why he's doing it again, his imposter syndrome and how he thinks about it.

chunks.heading: Buildspace's legacy inside the batch
chunks.text:
- Many founders in the batch told him they credit being at YC to buildspace, his earlier company.
- One example: a founder showed him a selfie of the two of them at a buildspace event when the founder was 15. That founder is now 18 and in the same batch.
- Some people who saw him in person assumed he was joining as a YC partner. They were surprised he was joining as a founder "back in the dirt alongside them."
- He says he often struggles to stop and appreciate the value of past work because he is so focused on the future, so this was a welcome moment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains why he and his cofounder nearly pivoted Tidbit, then refocused on single-player consumer after realizing B2B wasn't energizing them. He covers time-boxed bets, rapid weekly rebuilds, TikTok content conversion numbers, and third-party validation of a cofounder pairing.

chunks.heading: Pivot discussions and finding the real "why"
chunks.text:
- Farza and cofounder Sharif had a long talk about potentially pivoting Tidbit even though it had "classic startup" green flags: paying users, a lot of attention, new users arriving daily. Neither felt drawn to the idea.
- After a weekend of thinking, Farza concluded Tidbit was still the best idea they had. They had just strayed from the original vision and needed to refocus. He texted Sharif that on Monday and Sharif agreed.
- His principle: "I think an idea should be able to survive a pivot discussion." If it does, it strengthens your confidence in the idea.
- When something feels wrong and you can't say what, a discussion doesn't hurt.

chunks.heading: Why B2B worked on paper but didn't fit
chunks.text:
- The week before, teams came in and tried the product. Farza and Sharif built what customers asked for: MCPs (PostHog, GitHub, Linear, some custom ones) and ways to collaborate on data with teammates.
- Example: a Tidbit channel with a PostHog MCP lets a non-technical teammate (Hasan, the content person) ask "how many people came from TikTok" without learning PostHog's event names. Farza can hop in to help prompt since it's multiplayer.
- Sales happened in DMs. Owen at Boardy had a custom MCP and was using Claude Desktop MCPs plus shared team folders. This was the classic "customer already hacked together a solution" signal, and it became a paying user.
- Farza saw the B2B path clearly: "Talk to customers, build what they want. Find 5-10 more. Repeat." He says he literally saw the path to $1M, then $10M.
- But he "stopped giving a shit so fast." He didn't care about custom MCPs, team dashboards or agentic webhook channels that save support time. He was waiting for customer calls to end.
- His rule: if he doesn't deeply care, he has little faith he'll build a good product. After his previous company, he is wary of work that depletes his energy. Sometimes you power through, but this early in a company he thinks he should be getting energy from it.
- On opportunity size: "what's the point of working on a $100M opportunity if I'm not motivated about the opportunity itself? I probably won't even make it far + give up."

chunks.heading: Returning to the guiding light: build what you use daily
chunks.text:
- Farza and Sharif realized they were no longer building a product they used daily, which was their number one guiding light. Customers could be made happy, but they had lost sight of why they were building it.
- They want to build for consumers: people like their parents, friends and past coworkers.
- The analytics backed this up. The heaviest users were normal people using the long-context feature for everything from #copywriting to #therapy to #tiktok-scripts. A text from Alec, founder of an app studio, reinforced it.
- They dialed back "multiplayer" and refocused on single-player consumer.
- New one-liner: "Tidbit is an interface for power users of Claude."
- Result: better ideas, better energy, more smiling, "naturally obsessed," more bullish.

chunks.heading: Product direction: long-context memory and channels
chunks.text:
- The problem: people want Claude and GPT to retain context across sessions and build on previous work instead of "having amnesia every time." This matters most for content creation, research and any work of constantly refining ideas.
- Channels were kept, but got messy without a thread interface, so Sharif built threads. A channel like #design remembers past chats, so asking for inspiration on a new UI references past UIs he liked or disliked.
- Building ChatGPT and Claude imports: one click brings all conversations into Tidbit so users feel channels plus long-context memory immediately.
- Plan: launch it together with small features and a new landing page the following week.

chunks.heading: Shipping philosophy for a final-week swing
chunks.text:
- With 7 days left before re-evaluating, the team decided to take "a massive swing."
- Farza's stance: "We rather the app looking massively different each week and we test new hypotheses vs make a bunch of small incremental changes over a longer period on a flawed hypothesis."
- Schedule: 6 days on, 1 day off, always Sunday off no matter what, office locked.

chunks.heading: TikTok content experiment
chunks.text:
- Hasan, the content person, got almost 4,000,000 views in 7 days, making about 3-5 TikToks a day. Some pop, some flop.
- Conversion (view profile, go to link, make account) is about 0.5% on super Tidbit-specific content. Meme and trend content converts much lower but "juices algo."
- TikToks also get reposted by others on Instagram and gain results there.
- Farza says the content is unlike anything he'd have thought of himself. He trusts Hasan and treats the team as "actor bots" for him. So far it's working.
- Conversion takes time, but he is pleased with early numbers.

chunks.heading: Cofounder fit and the team plan
chunks.text:
- Farza and Sharif visited YC and spoke with Aaron Epstein, who worked with Sharif in 2019 and Farza in 2020. Aaron told them: "I think you two should just work together forever," and explained how they balance each other emotionally.
- Farza notes this was third-party validation from someone who has known them for years and seen thousands of founders. It wasn't needed, but it boosted their confidence as a duo.
- Plan: after the final week, a roughly 2-week break (after about 3 months non-stop), then decide whether to keep doing Tidbit and whether to keep working together.
- Kamil (engineer) and Hasan (content) were on a planned 30-day speed-run and become free agents afterward.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza's weekly update on Tidbit, a multiplayer AI chat product. He covers setting one daily A+ goal for the team, pivoting positioning from "replace Slack" to "work better with AI" without changing the product, shipping webhooks and MCPs, and switching short-form video from Reels to TikTok to land B2B customers.

chunks.heading: Tidbit's week: daily A+ goals, a messaging pivot, and moving from Instagram Reels to TikTok
chunks.text:
Farza describes a single week of Tidbit (an AI product with shared team chat) when it had three weeks left before its future was decided.

**Daily A+ goal and a win/loss board**
- Farza set one "A+" goal per day for the whole team and judged each day a win or a loss against it. The week ended with 5 W days and 2 L days.
- Monday's A+ was "ship a link to the app to Michael (Cursor) + Ivan (Notion)", the two founders who had asked to use Tidbit. The Notion CEO had already paid the $99 a month.
- The team shipped it by end of day Monday, after delaying the new version for a while while working on reliability, a team-invite flow and a desktop app. Farza's note on it: "we turned our brains off and shipped."
- His reasoning: "I really hate going home and not knowing if I won or lost." A clear result lets him come back and play harder after a win, or step back and set a better goal after a loss. He says the in-between state is the bad one: "I get sad when its in the middle."
- He says "an intense deadline with the right goal can feel so good."

**Results after the Monday ship**
- About 300 teams on the free tier.
- About 35 paying teams at $99 a month.
- Farza emailed the paying teams and posted a tweet that brought in more teams.

**Why simple tweets work**
- He argues that simple tweets are "extremely underrated". His example: a tweet built around how people feel about Slack drew almost 100 DMs.
- His view is that a plain "if you wanna try Tidbit drop a reply" would not have produced as many good leads: "No one gives a shit about Tidbit. But, everyone knows how they feel when they think of Slack."

**Messaging pivot: from "replace Slack" to "work better with AI"**
- The DMs made him realize "Tidbit kinda sucks as a Slack/Discord competitor." The team noticed this internally too, and saw new users sign up and churn.
- The value people actually felt was collaborating with the AI on a very specific problem together. His example: he and Hasan coming up with a TikTok idea with the model in the same chat.
- He dropped the "do all your work chat here as well" and "ditch Slack" narrative and reframed Tidbit around "work better with AI".
- He treats this as a messaging pivot, not a product pivot. The change was a few words on the landing page and in the DMs he sent.
- His principle: in the early days, nail the messaging. "Sometimes, it's up just setting up messaging properly so the emotion people enter the tool with is a hyper-specific one."
- Method for picking the angle: find (1) the most exciting angle for the team, (2) the angles people are most excited about, and combine them. He judged the messaging to be "getting better and better every week."

**New features: webhooks and basic MCPs**
- Tidbit users were already hacking the product to pipe external data into channels and work on it alongside Claude, so the team shipped a simple way to do it:
  1. Create a channel.
  2. Add a system prompt telling Claude what to do when a new webhook arrives.
- The example setup: a webhook fires every time someone fills out the access form on the landing page and goes to #new-users. The channel's system prompt tells Claude to research the signup from their email or company using web search, judge whether they are interesting or a big potential customer, and if so write a personalized email from Sharif's point of view scheduling a call.
- Tidbit has web search and recursive tool calling, so Claude can run several searches to dig deeper into someone's background.
- Farza was already doing this by hand: he Googled each new user to decide whether to learn more. Now an agent does it, and he wakes up to a message telling him which signups have the most revenue potential. It correctly flagged a legitimate marketing agency as a serious user worth a call.
- Emails can be sent from inside Tidbit through the Gmail MCP. He clicks "Send, Edit, or Decline" to tell the AI what to do.
- He can also ask Claude questions in the chat about the incoming user data.
- Because Tidbit is multiplayer, Sharif can step in to control the agent and who it contacts, and the whole team can see what the agents are doing.
- Further agents he describes: one for #hiring to track strong engineers who reach out, and one for #stripe that alerts him when someone notable starts a trial.

**Moving from Instagram Reels to TikTok**
- He and Hasan pivoted off IG Reels. They felt they were trying too hard to tell a story that was not there yet, and the "tell a story about what I'm building" format felt wrong.
- Hasan was only there for three more weeks. Farza calls it naive to think they could craft a new storytelling style in four weeks, since that would take at least 3-4 months. What they wanted was people flooding into Tidbit.
- He rejects the idea that short-form video is the same across platforms: "TikTok has an extremely different culture."
- On TikTok they started getting their first B2B customers: agencies, consulting firms and founders ("yes, they are all on TikTok").
- Cadence: 3-4 TikToks a day. Hasan holds the camera and hands Farza a script, and Farza just delivers it. His takeaway: "It's good to trust your team." Sharif also started making TikToks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains why he and Sharif used a live stream with a hard deadline to get Tidbit's first customers. He sets a small goal (10 paying teams), picks the narrative first, builds a simple landing page around it, and values the right audience over big view counts. The stream got 14 customers from about 14,000 views.

chunks.heading: Why Farza ran a live stream instead of a launch for Tidbit
chunks.text:
Farza and his co-founder Sharif ran a live stream to force Tidbit out the door. Farza states two reasons.

- He is fatigued by "launches" and rarely converts on them. He says he has not watched a company's launch video in months.
- He "actually despise[s] launch culture in 2025" and misses "the 2016 vibes of people just putting stuff out they were jamming on."
- He and Sharif like deadlines that can't be pushed, because missing one means embarrassing themselves. "Forcing functions are good."

chunks.heading: Goal for the stream: 10 paying teams and a good demo
chunks.text:
- The target was to find 10 legit teams willing to pay $99 a month, plus give a good demo.
- He admits they could have reached 10 teams by messaging friends or emailing potential users. He found that boring: "if we're not into it, we'll likely do bad work."
- Result: 14 customers, and a demo he called fun.
- Next step: make those 14 "really, really happy." Then "14 can turn into 28, and 28 to 56."

chunks.heading: Splitting the work between co-founders
chunks.text:
- Sharif went all in on preparing the product for the stream.
- Farza went all in on making noise, working out why the stream would be interesting, and getting people to show up.
- Each trusted the other to deliver.
- As a former solo founder, he had to hold everything in his head at once, which "riddled me with anxiety." This split let him focus on what he loved doing.

chunks.heading: Deciding the narrative first
chunks.text:
- Farza treats streams, launches, tweets, shorts and every touchpoint as "the narrative."
- He decides the narrative before anything else. If it isn't clear and compelling, the audience gets confused and loses interest.
- He wants narratives that are easy to latch onto and easy to tell friends.
- "I never make up narratives." The narrative is usually already in front of him, and he just puts it into words.
- The obvious question was why anyone would attend a 45-minute midweek stream for a barely working product.
- The answer was the real story: two guys, a few weeks in, still unsure, trying to make some magic.
- He wrote one clarifying sentence, then derived everything from it: the landing page, invites, tweets, stream look, and how the product would be presented.

chunks.heading: Low-key promotion and the audience Farza wanted
chunks.text:
- He built a simple landing page for the stream.
- He made a few tweets and posts on Instagram and LinkedIn, emailed people who downloaded Freewrite, and dropped messages in a few WhatsApp groups. It was mostly word of mouth.
- He knew a tweet like "come to our livestream" would flop because of audience fatigue, so he stuck to the narrative instead.
- About 1,000 people RSVPed.
- He prefers 25 attendees who care over 2,500 who are barely listening.
- He criticizes founders chasing virality and numbers instead of "people that can help them build a better product + be a part of their true audience."
- He would rather find 10 people who "genuinely give a fuck," believe in the core idea and will iterate with him than get 1,000 likes on a tweet or 1M views on a video.
- His gut call was that if 100 people thought the product was cool, they would drive 1,000 people to the recording.

chunks.heading: Stream production: roughly 8 hours of setup
chunks.text:
- He cut a simple waiting room from old footage of himself and Sharif in Japan.
- A friend, Josh, helped fix his camera setup (his settings had been poor for months) and set basic lighting and framing.
- He spent a few hours on the stream narrative and flow: what to show, what order, and what keeps people excited.
- He put the plan in an Apple Note and rehearsed it with Sharif the morning of the stream.

chunks.heading: Writing the conversion page: headlines and copy
chunks.text:
- The question was how to turn stream interest into leads and sign-ups, and which headline would convert teams.
- Candidate headlines were "Claude for your team," "Claude, but, multiplayer" and "Your third co-founder." None felt strong, and he says he wouldn't convert on any of them.
- Farza and Sharif had been discussing an ideal where Tidbit is the only place a team chats and works alongside AI models, so Slack is no longer needed. Farza loved that it felt "new, different, direct."
- He took the landing page copy from 2015 Discord's landing page, which felt punchy and direct. Discord's enemy was TeamSpeak, and Tidbit paints Slack as the enemy.
- He may not keep that messaging long term, but it lets them test teams messaging aggressively.
- He keeps a diary of phrases he loves, such as "In Tidbit, Claude sits in your teams conversations." and "We want it to feel like you have this genius third co-worker you never even knew."

chunks.heading: Using the product itself to write the letter
chunks.text:
- Farza and Sharif keep a #user-convos channel in Tidbit with every user call transcript, interesting quote and interesting DM.
- He gave Tidbit a screenshot of the old hey.com launch letter and asked it to write a similar letter about what they were building.
- The draft drew on real examples from users that he had forgotten about.
- One generated line: "When your cofounder talks about new pricing models, Claude might chime in with an insight."
- His lesson: "When AI has deep context, it performs really well." When the founders are impressed by their own tool, he treats that as a good sign.
- He generated several letters, picked his favorite pieces, ran them by Sharif, and wrote the final section.
- The conversion section gave two options: pay $99, or tell us you're broke. He likes giving users funny choices.
- His test: "it felt like a landing page I'd convert on for $99 a month. If I wouldn't convert on it no one else would."

chunks.heading: Results and why 14,000 views was enough
chunks.text:
- The stream got 13,000 views on Twitter and 1,800 on YouTube Live, about 14,000 total.
- He says he has gone viral a bunch, but cares about "the 'right' views" at this stage.
- "I've made stuff that gets 1M views and 10 sign ups. It sucks."
- Views alone don't equal success. Success is a true audience, "a true group of people that give a shit."
- The viewers were mostly people curious about the product, founders with teams, ambitious people curious how AI models change teamwork, and friends.
- "Our DMs were full of the people we wanted to be hearing from."
- The stream forced "a lot of clarity" out of him and Sharif in a short time. Their goal is to keep clarifying the idea in a focused way and fast: "Every single day counts."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza recounts finding a co-founder in Sharif after five years solo, then flying to Tokyo with no idea to build. Daily prototypes, one-liner tweets, demo-driven development and rapid user calls turned into a product with paying customers and 1000+ DMs in two weeks.

chunks.heading: Why Farza went looking for a co-founder, and who Sharif is
chunks.text:
- By mid-2025 Farza was tired of building alone: "I just wasn't having fun. And if I'm not having fun I don't think I'll build good things." He gets a lot of energy from working with others.
- He had been a solo founder for about 5 years (kanga, zipschool, buildspace). He calls those years painful and says they took a lot of "mental gymnastics" to stay sane.
- He wrote a note describing the person he wanted (farza.com/cofounder) and sent it to 15 friends who might know someone. He expected nothing from it, but figured he would learn something about himself.
- Sharif Shameem, one of the 15, replied that he wanted to work together. They met roughly a decade earlier through a HackerNews post: Farza was 21 and training AI models for video games, and Sharif was 19 and had just launched the GPU product VectorDash.
- They roomed together in SF and stayed close friends for about 7 years, but never worked together. Farza says the reasons were timing and maturity: at 21 he had a massive ego and "was an ass", and it took him a very long time to learn to work with others.
- Now 29 and 27, they were both comfortable with direct personal feedback, which made working together easy.

chunks.heading: Changing environment to find an idea: 14 days in Japan with no plan
chunks.text:
- They decided on a Sunday, flew to Japan on Tuesday, and had no product idea. They went because they like Japan, and because they believe changing your environment produces new ideas.
- Their shared philosophy is "you gotta try stuff to find stuff", so the plan was to "aggressively try stuff."
- Setup: a quiet suburb of Tokyo (Setagaya City) with a nearby supermarket for pre-made food (lots of yakitori), so no time went to cooking or logistics. They worked from the apartment, Denny's and local cafes, and were the only foreigners in the area.
- Day 1: each prototyped something alone from 9AM, then they demoed to each other at 3PM.
  - Sharif built a desktop app that looked like ChatGPT but with Discord-style channels.
  - Farza built a Discord bot where two people prompt the model together and do real work alongside it. They wrote the title of his YouTube video this way, with Claude.
  - The bot was "quite bad" at first, but "the vibe was there", and they found it fun to generate ideas together with AI.

chunks.heading: Aligning on a vision: one-liners and launch tweets
chunks.text:
- They merged the two prototypes (channels plus a multiplayer interface for models) by drafting many one-liners and potential launch tweets.
- Test for being on the same page: if the idea can be said in one line, or sounds exciting as a tweet, they agree. Then they "worked backwards from the one-liner" and built.
- The product became Tidbit, described as "like ChatGPT, but, with channels."

chunks.heading: Daily operating rhythm and working-together hygiene
chunks.text:
- Every morning around 9AM they spent 30-60 minutes deciding what to finish by 9PM, then tried to do exactly that.
- The same check-in covered how they were working together. They raised and resolved any friction immediately. Since they had never worked together, Farza calls these check-ins "extremely important."
- By about Day 5 the trip's main goal was clear: build a product they love using. If they returned to SF with something they used every day, that was "a massive win."
- Most of the code was written by Claude Code, and both of them coded a lot. Farza says the cost showed up back in SF: "Claude just stacks technical debt."

chunks.heading: Demo-driven development and shameless public shipping
chunks.text:
- They agreed to post daily demos right away and not care about polish, "optimizing for learnings. Not a user number, or a graph, or a money number."
- Demos forced them to get their thoughts in order. They didn't want to put out "absolute shit", but a demo was always fine.
- Day 5: the first demo went on Sharif's Twitter and did well. A few friends showed interest, which gave them a push when they still didn't know if the idea mattered.
- A day later they shipped a second demo on Farza's Twitter, recorded around midnight while jet-lagged. This one focused on the channel aspect, and "momentum just came."
- Result: about 1000+ DMs combined. Interest came from founders using it with teams or co-founders, college students collaborating, people planning trips with family or friends, and ChatGPT/Claude power-users tired of re-explaining themselves to Claude.
- Many of these use cases were ones they had never thought of: "people were coming up with the product for us."
- Some people just DM'd "Access", and he gave them access anyway.

chunks.heading: Turning attention into learning: user calls and a fast loop
chunks.text:
- Once there was clear interest, Farza booked about 20 user calls while Sharif improved the product "every 2-hours." They sat next to each other 24/7.
- The goal of the calls was to learn why people were excited. Showing the product and talking to people "prompts my brain in new ways and gives me ideas."
- He ran a mix of experiments:
  - Gave some people free access and tracked them closely in PostHog.
  - Sent others a Stripe link in the DMs before the call.
- He describes this as random, with the aim of learning rather than any single metric.
- Findings: users wanted longer-context conversations and were tired of re-explaining themselves to Claude/GPT. Teams wanted to collaborate with each other and the model instead of passing GPT and Claude links around Slack.
- Outcome after 14 days: paying customers, users, a lot of attention, a product they were excited about, and clarity. Next steps were applying the feedback and running about 25 more user calls on the same loop.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza shares what he learned in his first 21 days starting over: no rules except show up daily and make something to show one person. Small, fun, unplanned projects (a text editor, a YouTube video, a voice agent) outperformed expectations, and showing work early fuels better ideas.

chunks.heading: Showing up daily with two rules, shipping to one person
chunks.text:
- Farza started from zero in April 2025 and describes his first 21 days as "good, but fucking difficult."
- He has no rules about what to build. Some days he picks a new thing (a VR game), some days he continues a prior project.
- He is "insanely, stupidly disciplined" about exactly two things:
  - Show up every day.
  - Make something and show at least one person.
- Most days he starts at a blank page. He says he's not "that guy that has like 1000 ideas on an Apple Note."
- Day 1 was full of anxiety. For the first 5 hours he thought everything he did was stupid. Around hour 8 he started a simple text editor for himself, built the first version in 4 hours, and texted a rough Xcode build ZIP to a friend.
- He says he trusts his process, and that the two rules force output even when motivation and ideas are absent.

chunks.heading: Shipping small and embarrassing things anyway (Freewrite text editor)
chunks.text:
- By the end of week 1 he thought the editor was "kinda cool" but was embarrassed that it was simple, small, and niche.
- He decided to ignore what people might say and ship it. He asked a collaborator (Josh) to make a launch video in two hours.
- He chose a video not to go viral or look cool; it had no rationale: "I just did it because it seemed fun." About 95% of the reason was that he likes working with Josh.
- Expectation: he'd have been happy with 10 downloads.
- Result: 1.8M views on X, thousands of downloads, and a community of "die-hard Freewrite fans" whose feedback he found heart-warming.
- Lesson he draws: low expectations plus fun and shipping beats waiting until something feels impressive.

chunks.heading: Making a YouTube video end to end in one day
chunks.text:
- He messaged a collaborator (Aiden) about a day before and made the whole video in one day: script, shooting, editing, thumbnail.
- Expectations were zero. He'd have been happy with 100 views; the goal was "to get off 0 on YT."
- Results: almost half a million views across platforms (X, LinkedIn, YouTube), with 25,000 views on YouTube. About 75% of YouTube views came from the algorithm.
- He pushes back on the idea that he has a master plan for a "personal brand." He made it because it seemed fun and he wanted to work with Aiden again.
- Plan going forward: try to make 1 video per month for YouTube.

chunks.heading: Turning user learnings into a new product (voice agent)
chunks.text:
- In week 3 he started a voice agent to help him talk through his day. It came from watching Freewrite users: people loved the AI feature he added last minute.
- His reasoning: "what if that was one entire product." He thought it was a stupid idea, but had no other ideas that Tuesday and had to ship something.
- Build, in about 3 hours:
  - Learned iOS/Expo.
  - Made the initial UI.
  - Added real-time voice with ElevenLabs and conversation with Gemini Flash.
  - Demoed a grandpa giving advice.
  - He admits he "literally ripped off" an ElevenLabs Expo React Native cookbook blog post and changed the background.
- He walked around the office showing the rough demo to about 20 people and was surprised by how some people spoke to it.
- For the next 2 days he improved it a little each day and showed 10-20 people each update. He now has "a ton" of ideas for something he first thought was stupid.
- Takeaway: "Just gotta ship. Just gotta show people."

chunks.heading: Put users in one group chat and mine it for ideas
chunks.text:
- Tactic: "adding your users to a single GC is always a good idea."
- He learns a lot from watching how people talk about the product. The Freewrite group chat had grown to 1k people and gives him "an insane amount of new ideas."
- The voice agent was directly inspired by learnings from this user base.

chunks.heading: How ideas actually get generated: show people, react to their reactions
chunks.text:
- His best ideas come from showing someone something, hearing their thoughts, and having that trigger a new idea. He describes the feeling of "you're on to something."
- His main goal for the first 3 weeks was to flex that muscle: build something small, show it, iterate on the reaction.
- His brain keeps building on prior days' work rather than starting from a blank slate each day (example: the voice agent came out of Freewrite user learnings). If he has to start blank each day, he'll keep doing it.
- He keeps things "loose as hell" with no rules, backed by a good level of base focus.

chunks.heading: Build with other people, even briefly
chunks.text:
- Learning one: build with others even if only for 30 minutes and even if he barely knows what he's building.
- Examples of small collaborations: Josh and Aiden on videos, Dante on a YouTube thumbnail, Stavan on tweet copy, Jack on voice agent implementation.
- Why: these gave him energy, made him feel less alone, and made his ideas better.
- He notes you can work with friends in small ways and have fun; "it doesn't have to be all-in or nothing."

chunks.heading: Building a mental game for starting over
chunks.text:
- Learning two: spending the previous 8 months deliberately building a new "mental" was worth it. He had told no one about this.
- Components: updated internal rules, new internal motivations, and new strategies for dealing with his mind. His goal was that his mental would never fail him again.
- He is very emotional (smiles, laughs, cries, and gets anxious easily) and wants to keep feeling all emotions because they make him feel alive and lead to his best work: "It's hard to be creative without being deeply in touch with your emotions."
- The goal was that emotions no longer change his state of mind while he works.
- The first 3 weeks were the test. Result: a majority of days were happy; emotions rarely controlled him; on down days he knew how to rebound. He called it a real personal breakthrough and said the challenge is maintaining it as things get bigger.

chunks.heading: Funding and pacing notes
chunks.text:
- He raised two small checks from friends: Furqan and Hubert at Founders Inc, and Ryan at Weekend Fund. He kept it "extremely low key."
- He took a day off, went 3 hours north to a cabin, and enjoyed nature as part of staying sustainable.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza explains why chasing investors early is a focus sinkhole, but ignoring capital entirely is also a mistake. His answer is to consistently "tell the world" over 12-24 months, especially via a weekly progress newsletter that builds trust with a small audience who may later fund you.

chunks.heading: Why Farza avoids the fundraising topic but doesn't ignore it
chunks.text:
- At buildspace, Farza usually stays away from raising money or finding investors. His focus is showing people how to make stuff.
- He sees alumni raise $50K-$500K nearly every week. His view: "If you ship, tell the world, repeat... capital finds its way to you." He adds that it isn't guaranteed.
- Chasing investors early can be "a terrible sinkhole for focus". Builders go from making cool products to "methodically begging others for money".
- He also thinks fully ignoring the money world is a mistake. The goal is to set yourself up to "get lucky" and possibly pursue investors later.

chunks.heading: What the builders who raise money have in common
chunks.text:
- The alumni who raise money "magically" (a $25K grant, a small angel check) are usually very good at "telling the world" consistently over a long horizon, roughly 12-24 months.
- A one-off viral Twitter demo or a single Reddit blowup doesn't count. Those are hard to control and disappear fast.
- The real asset is trust built with an audience over a long time.

chunks.heading: The weekly newsletter as the most underrated way to tell your story
chunks.text:
- Farza says writing a newsletter each week with your progress is the most underrated way to tell your story, and he can't believe every builder doesn't do it.
- Content can be anything: things you tried that week, how you're thinking about your work, how you're feeling.
- He wrote his every week for nearly 3 years (2017-2020), almost 150 issues. They covered his emotions and how he analyzed different markets to decide what to work on, giving readers a view into his head every week.
- He assumed no one cared and wrote it mainly so his Mom could understand what he was doing.

chunks.heading: What the newsletter produced
chunks.text:
- The list had only 125 people after 3 years.
- Those readers deeply understood him and his journey. When he needed $25,000 to start buildspace, he got it from one person on that newsletter.
- Lesson: you don't need a big audience, you need a small one that follows your story over time.

chunks.heading: Why owned formats beat tweets
chunks.text:
- Farza sees builders tweet something, watch it not blow up, and move on. His objection is that Twitter is "extremely ephemeral" and your story fades quickly.
- A newsletter or blog shows people your long-term history and lets you communicate more thoroughly.
- Alternatives work too. Some builders send him a monthly YouTube vlog on what they did that month. His advice: "Do whatever, just please tell your story."

chunks.heading: Mindset: your story matters
chunks.text:
- "Your story matters. It's just your job to package it up nicely for others to also be a part of it."
- You never know who may read it.
- If you think you have nothing to say, he says you're lying, because you're living the story right now. It just takes practice to tell it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Farza writes a personal update after six months of travel following the end of buildspace. It contains no growth, marketing or pricing tactics, only a reflection on burnout, feeling like a flop, and rediscovering the joy of making things. Low durable business insight beyond a mindset lesson.

chunks.heading: Stepping away after a company ends
chunks.text:
- After his company ended, Farza took a one-way flight out of SF with no plan. He didn't know if he would ever come back.
- He spent six months in places he describes as some of the most peaceful on the planet: villages in Morocco, remote forests in the Czech Republic, and the outskirts of Islamabad.
- He listened to a lot of the Beatles, spent most days doing nothing, and met "some wise people on the road".
- His caveat: "you don't just get on a plane and have your problems disappear."

chunks.heading: The low point: feeling like a flop
chunks.text:
- When the company ended, fans, friends and investors sent an overflow of support along the lines of "it was a good run. you gave it your best."
- Farza notes that "you are always your worst critic." For most of the trip he felt sad, tired and confused all at once.
- He felt like a flop and wondered whether he had really burned out and whether "the story ends here."
- What scared him most was the thought that he would never feel the love of building again, as if the spark he'd had since age 13 was "gone forever." He calls that "the worst."

chunks.heading: Recovery came from time, not a fix
chunks.text:
- His explanation for getting better is plain: "time just did what time does."
- By Feb 2025 he reported feeling "happier than ever" and "more excited than ever."
- He says the light came back while he was on the road. He describes finding again "the kid that see's the world as brand new and just wants to make cool things."
- He says the full story will come "one day" and jokes that it did not involve acid.

chunks.heading: Coming back to building
chunks.text:
- By the time of the post (Feb 20, 2025) Farza was back in SF, living 5 minutes from the office, and "falling in love with making things again."
- His summary: "i really feel 13 again." He says he is ready to "build something really fucking cool again" and adds "i'm not done yet."
- He was hacking on new ideas every day and invited people in SF who wanted to work together to get in touch and meet up.
- He thanked the thousands of people who messaged or tagged him during the break. He didn't have it in him to reply, but says it "meant more than you'll ever know."

chunks.heading: How he uses his channels
chunks.text:
- Farza posted the essay on X and on Substack. He thinks Twitter is "decent for long form," but sometimes a piece also deserves its own post on Substack.
- He describes Twitter, Substack and his blog as usually "polished."
- He was enjoying Instagram for "more personal, day to day stuff" and invited people to follow him there.

We usually stay away from the topic of raising money or finding investors -- we just wanna show you how to make stuff.

Yet, every week I see a new @_buildspace alumni raise $50K - $500K.

Yes. If you ship, tell the world, repeat... capital finds it's way to you.

But, it's not guaranteed (nothing is).

The reason I stay away from the topic is because I know chasing investors early on can often just be a terrible sinkhole for focus.

Most know this.

You go from making cool products -- to methodically begging others for money.

But, I also don't think fully ignoring the money world is good either, you wanna set yourself up to get lucky + potentially pursue investors.

So -- how do you do that.

Those I see from buildspace that end up raising money magically, scoring a $25K grant, getting a small angel check, whatever often are just really good at "telling the world" consistently over a long horizon (ex. 12-24 months).

I don't mean going viral on Twitter with a demo or blowing up on Reddit once -- these are difficult to control + disappear fast.

You wanna build trust with an audience over a long time.

The most underrated way to "tell the world" your story is simply by writing a newsletter each week with your progress.

This is something I can't believe every builder doesn't just do.

Write about things you tried that week, how you're thinking about your work, how you're feeling, literally whatever.

I wrote mine every week for nearly 3-years, that's nearly 150 newsletters.

It covered everything from the deep dark trenches of my emotions to how I analyzed different markets to decide what to work on. It gave people a view into my head, every week.

Tbh, I thought no one cared and I mainly wrote it for my Mom to help her understand what I was doing (lol).

But, I had 125 people on the list after 3-years (2017 - 2020).

I ended up building an audience of people that deeply understood me + my journey -- and when one day I needed $25,000 to start this company, I ended up getting it from one person on that newsletter.

Your story matters.

It's just your job to package it up nicely for others to also be a part of it.

I often see builders tweet stuff, and then it doesn't blow up, and they move on but issue is Twitter is extremely ephemeral -- your story fades away quickly.

Something like a newsletter, blog, etc helps people see your long-term history + lets you communicate more thoroughly.

I also have some builders who literally send me a YouTube vlog once a month covering what they did that month.

Do whatever, just please tell your story.

You never know who may read it.

And if you think you have nothing to say you are lying -- because you're living the story right now.

Just takes some practice to tell it.
